ILLUSTRATED FASHIONS.

Fashion is displaying more common sense this season than in those immediately preceding, and one of the strongest outward tokens is •evinced in the fact that walking skirts are of a more abbreviated and, therefore, more manageable length than heretofore. Some very smart gowns indeed are worn with the skirt cub just to clear the ground all round. This evolution of fashion which has led to such exceedingly sensible changes has been so gradual as to be hardly perceptible, but now that it has become fashion- able to be comfortable a weight will be lifted from off the minds of those women who will follow the modes blindly and to any extreme. and they can suit their garments to themselves in a manner to which they have long been strangers.

IN charming indecision she gazed at the two por- traits. The uncertainty in her heart clouded hei eyes just enough to soften and render more be- witching their splendour. " Which shall it be ?" she murmured. From one to the other of the pictures her glance wandered. Now her counte- nance would for a moment beam with the joy of a settled choice, only to darken again in a moment with perplexity. "It I could only say which one !" A sigh fluttered within the tender bosom and escaped from the rosy lips. "Will is dark. I love dark men." She clasped her hands, and rap- turously scrutinised the nearest portrait. "But Henry is noble and good." A faint flush crept into her cheeks. Her thoughts were with the other ,picture. " One; of them I must marry." Rising to her feet, she paced the floor ner- vously. It was a life's happiness that hung trembling in the balance. "I am sure both of them love me with all their hearts." Hand was pressed in hand, until the blood forsook the taper fingers with the frantic pressure. "Both of them—but stay !" It was a startled look that flashed across her face. "Yes, yes, it is surely so." Belief succeeded anxiety, and a smile of sweet content fluttered about her lips. "If I marry Will, Henry"—She leaned forward fondly towards the portraits. "Henry will give me a wedding present. If I marry Henry, I just know Will would be huffy and never give me a thing." She pondered a moment in silence. "Yes," she softly whispered at last, ''l shall marry ill." High resolve invested her _-Rrsonalitv with a new interest. The Most Nutritious.

mode with box-pleats stitched flat to just below the knee, where a considerable amount of fulness is permitted to spring out. Of course a skirt of this description js innocent of a train proper and must not be allowed to more than rest upon the ground at the back, otherwise it will become unmanageable in muddy weather. The costume is completed by a wide hat of felt with a fur-bordered brim and a velvet crown. The whole is finished off by a handsome fur necklet of the flat variety trimmed with clusters of tails.

Many and various to a degree are the materials in vogue and some very fanciful shot cloths and chine woollens are new, but anything that is very striking is sure soon to become weari- some to the eye. Plain materials are really the most elegant, and besides make the best back- grounds to the rich embroideries which with lace and strappings form the most fashionable trimmings. Long-haired zibelines and white flecked woollens figure prominently among the novelties in materials, but this fashion for rough-surfaced long-haired fabrics is perhaps rather inclined to be overdone, and therefore the best-dressed women will probably remain faithful to the fine-face cloth which always looks well and falls in such perfect draperies. The pretty and becoming hat depicted is trimmed with a narrow band of ermine at

either edge of the wide np-turned brim, while a long ostrich feather curls over the hair at the back in a pictnresque manner. 1.

There is a splendid opportunity this season for the home-milliner to give scope to her talents, for there are so many hats which only require a smartly-arranged bow or well-placed feather to ensure their success, for in them- selves they are of a somewhat elaborate descrip- tion. There are some untrimmed shapes made entirely of birds' feathers placed smoothly so as to overlap each other, while others again are a good imitation of astrachan' besides being much lighter to wear than the fur itself. A very smart hat I admired recently was of the toreador variety in white felt, with the brim bound with black velvet, the sole trimming consisting of a group of white marabout pom- poms tipped with small black feathers, while a bandeau and depending ends of black velvet ribbon formed the reteke-peigne at the back. The effect was really very good, and one which is particularly easily obtained.

The pretty afternoon blouse illustrated is made of cream viyella trimmed with a collar of richly-hued embroidery, the same embroidery lining the turned back corners and forming the cuffs of the full-wristed sleeves. It is made with a drawn front of cream silk, and the neck is finished by a small turn-over collar and a

BLOUSE. ribbon tie of bright green silk which matches some ot the predominating tones of the em- broidery. Two large enamelled buttons catch the corners of the collar and the same appear lower down. while two groups of three gold buttons grace the edge. The claims of the woollen blouse are always felt at this season of the year, and one can do well with one of flannel made in the shirt-blouse style for morning wear and another of a more elaborate description for the afternoon. Even the simplest blouses nowadays are made with some sort of elaboration, which generally takes the form of tuckings. Frequently little groups of ornamen- tal buttons are introduced on blouses with good effect. Indeed buttons and ribbons, which a few seasons ago were regarded with little or no Interest, are now in great demand for trimming every article of dress.
COQUETTE,

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT,
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT,

The appearance of the Christmas numbers, romiods us that the festive season is not far off, and those who do much in giving away presents, are already planning out their selections. Those for triends abroad, have mo&tl7 to be sent off this month, and what with the making ot tho puddings, housewives will soon be busy with their preparations. Fruit and groceries premise to be fairly cheap this year, but it is said there will be a grest scarcity of mistletoe that popular item in the Christmas decorations, Large quantities have hitherto c, me from Normandy and Brittany, but the French Government have recently required all mistletoe to be destroyed, owing to the damage caused to the orchards, and this it is thought will greatly reduce our supplies of the plant next month.

The Church Society for Promoting Kindness to Animals is one of those benevolent aasociations which are trying to do by moral suasion what ought to be done by the Legislature. The annual report tells the old story of wanton cruelty towards the brute creation, and the Society attributes any of our reverses in the war to want of proper concern for the well-being of animals. On the other hand, the Society find matter for congratu- lation in the introduction of motor traction, to which they look for a reduction in the amount of suffering which accompanies the life of the vast majority of horses. If the words " especially in the metropolis had been added ta this comment, there would not have been vary much injustice in the censure. Mrs Humphrey Ward, the well-known noveliet, is a Tasmanian by birth, she baying been born in Fobart in 1851. She is the gifted authoress of many books, each of which would have made ber famous, and she boa re- cently prepared a dramatised adaptation of "Eleanor which is now being played et the Court Theatre in London. Her most popular work however, was " Robert Elsmere " published in 1888, and it has since run through many editions, both in this country and in America. Possibly Mrs Ward may have inherited her great talents, for she is a granddaughter of Dr Arnold, the Read Master of Rugby, and a niece of the late Matthe* Arnold.

The National Union of Women Workers discussed many social questions at the conference in Edinburgh, including the relationship between marriage. The highly educated woman, as a rule, does net marry, and Miss Florence Melville stated that out of 500 women greduates belonging to Scotland, only nine per cent had married, whist) is less than a fourth of the average marriage rate. Various reasons were put forward to account for this state of things but they were mostly amplifications of two sets of opieion. Either the uni- versity woman was net sought after by marrying men, or else she usually had her awn purpose in life, which made her independent, and self-sufficient. No doubt both reasons account in some measure for the remark- able statistics which Miss Melville quoted, but it is Probably the latter that has the meet influence in this respect, seeing that a woman who had seriously fol- lowed up bar education,would hardly care to enter into partnership with a men who was, intellectually her inferior. But the most learned men sometimes take a romantic view of marriage, and MT Ruskin said that every girl ought to set her seven swains a task at chivalry, and make her choice accordingly. That of course, is an old• fashioned isles!, upon which the modern comment would be " first catch your seven swains " ; but it reminds ems of the many old time custom, which were practised by young men and maidens—generally at this time of the year to ascertain their matrimonial fate. There was the burning of ants on the festival of Hallow e'en,of which Burns has written in prase and in verse. There is also a similar charm for the first week in Advent designed to ascertain the name and disposition of the desired husband. So many onions are selected as there are eligible young men,and each ose named accordingly They are then placed in the chimney corner to force their growth, and the first one to sprout should identify the future husband. Then the plucking of a stick from a faggot was supposed to reveal his dispesition. If iz was straight sad without knots he weuld be all that was amiable, but if crooked and knotty, he would prove a churlish partner. The fashionable hour at which to be married is half. past two, and there is. happ,ly, no sign as yet of the much-talked-of revival of the heavy " breakfast." In the matter of bridesmaids, the number seems to increase every year, and it is no unusual thing to see twelve fair girls in attendance on the bride. Groomsmen are once more in request, and the ceremony over, each one soaks the" maid " entrusted to his care. Many fashionable brides have lately carried an ivory or mether-ef-pearl Prayer Book, instead of the bouquet, but in such instances there has been always the appearance of some- thing laeking about the toilet, which the flowers supply. Saturday is the favourite day for the important event, Tuesday and Thursday, respectively, coming nextin popularity.

The newest fans are quite small, a mixture of feathers, mounted on tortoiseshell sticks. When on fan has te de duty on all occasions,it is better to select an all black, or all white specimen, or a mixture of black and white, but when colours are worn, akal a fan—the feathers of which match the gown—is available, a very desirable air of completeness Is the result. The flannel shirt is a very different garment now-- days, to the dowdy blouse of a season or two back. The smartest this winter are in cream or white, spitted with black, and finished with a black tie. Many are bring made to fasten at the side, a dainty white cheMisette being donned with this variety. In colours, some ef the new flannels are extremely good-looking and smart, but plain black should he avoided, as even in the most skilful hands, black flannel is a hopeless fabric. That the little fur coat, which ends at the waist, is the cause of many a serious illness,in a certainty. Above his waist the wearer quickly becomes over-heated, and below contracts a chill. The danger may be lessened by the wearing of an extra underskirt, but even ao, it is great, The Woman who is sensible will ',tidy health first, and fashion last, and refuse to be garbed in the fur coat that finishes at the waist, choosing one that at any rate, covars the hips. Another important item is, fairly thick boots, for winter wear. Crld or damp feet are very often the Cause of serious illness, and should therefore be avoided. To cook rice successfully it must first he thorough.y washed in several waters, then thrown into a saucepan of boiling water,in which a little salt has been dissolved. Boil 1.4 minutes, pour a cupful of cold water on the rice, and strain in a collander. Place a smal knob of butter at the bottom of the saucepan, to welch the rice should be returned, and left on the stove to dry. .
MADGE.

He was appar- ently'in his usual hesll3, but stopping to ie a bootlace fell at the foot of tt e s'airs and died before he cou'd he moved, oresumatly frrm heart dhe.sr. div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
A DEAD FINGER,
BY S. BAILING GOULD, (Author of " Mehalah," "John Herring," &e.)
PART L

Why the National Gallery should not attract as many visitors as, say, the British Museum, I can- not explain. The latter does not contain much that, one would suppose, appealed to the interest of the ordinary sightseer. What knows such of pre- historic flints and scratched bones? Of Assyrian sculpture ? Of Egyptian hieroglyphics 1 The Greek and Roman statuary is cold and dead. The paintings in the national Gallery glow with colour, and are instinct with life. Yet, somehow, a few listless wanderers saunter yawning through the National Gallery, whereas swarms pour through the halls of the British Museum, and talk and pass remarks about the objects there exposed, of the date and meaning of which they have not the faintest conception. I was thinking of this problem, and endeavouring to unravel it, one morning whilst sitting in the- room for English masters at the great collection in Trafalgar Square. At the same time another thought forced itself upon me. I had been through the rooms deViated to foreign schools, and had then come into that given over to Reynolds, Moreland, Gainsborough, Constable, and Hogarth. The morning had been for a while propitious, but to- wards noon a dense umber-tinted fog had come on, making it all but impossible to see the pictures and quite impossible to do them justice. I was tired, and so seated myself on one of the chairs, and fell into the consideration first of all of---why the National Gallery is not as popular as it should be ; and secondly, how it was that the British School had no beginnings, like those of Italy and the Netherlands? We can see the art of the painter from its first initiation in the Italian peninsula, and among the Flemings. It starts on its progress like a child, and we can trace every stage okits growth. Not so with English art. It springs to life in full and splendid maturity. Who was there before Reynolds and Gainsborough and Hogarth ? The great names of those portrait and subject painters who have left their canvasses upon the walls of our country houses were those of fbreigners---Holbein, Knellet, Van Dyck, and Lely for portraits, and Monnoyer for flower and fruit pieces. Landscapes, figure subjects were all importations none home- grown. How came that about? importations, there no limner that was native? Was it that fashion trampled on home-grown pictorial beginnings as it flouted and spurned native music? Here was food for contemplation. Dreaming in the brown fog, looking through it without seeing its beauties, at Hogarth's painting of Lavinia Fenton as Polly Peachnon, without wondering how so indifferent a beauty could have captivated the Duke of Bolton and held him for thirty years, I was recalled to myself and my surroundings by the strange conduct of a lady who had seated herself on a chair near me, also discouraged by the fog, and awaiting its dispersion. I had not noticed her particularly. At the present moment I do not remember particularly what she was like. As far as I can recollect she was middle-aged, and was quietly, yet well dressed. It was not her face nor her dress that attracted my attention and disturbed the current of my thoughts; that which produced the effect I speak of was her strange movements and behaviour. / She had been sitting listless, probably thinking of nothing at all, or nothing in particular, when, in turning her eyes round, and finding that she could see nothing of the paintings, she began to study me. This did concern me greatly. A cat may look at a king; but to be contemplated by a lady is a compliment sufficient to please any gentleman. It was not gratified vanity that troubled my thoughts, but the consciousness that my appeAr- ance produced—first of all a startled surprise, then undisguised alarm, and, finally, indescribable horror. • Now a man can sit quietly leaning on the head of his umbrella, and glow internally, warmed and illumined by the consciousness that he is being sur- veyed with admiration by a lovely woman, even when he is middle-aged and not fashionably dressed; but no man can maintain his composure when he discovers himself to be an object of aversion and terror. .

What was it? I passed my hand over my chin and upper lip, thinking it not impossible that I might have forgotten to share that morning, and in my confusion not considering that the fog would prevent the lady from discovering my ,neglect in this particular, had it occurred, which it had not. I am a little careless, perhaps, about shaving when in the country; but when in town, never. The next idea that occurred to me was—a smut. Had a London black, 'Curdled in that dense pea- soup atmospheore, descended on my nose and blackened it? I hastily drew my, silk handker- chief from my pocket, moistened it, and passed it over my nose, and then each cheek. I then turned my eyes into the corners and looked at the lady, to see whether by this means I had got rid of what was objectionable in my personal appearance. Then I saw that her eyes, dilated with horror, were riveted, not on my face, but on my leg. My leg What• on earth could that harmless member have in it so terrifying? The morning had i been dull, there had been rain n the night, and I admit, in leaving my hotel, I had turned up the bottoms of my trousers. That is a proceeding not so uncommon, not so outrageous as to account for the stony stare of this woman's eyes. If that were all I would turn my trousers down. Then I saw her shrink from the chair on which she sat to one further removed from me, but still with her eyes fixed on my leg—about the level of my knee. She had let fall her umbrella, and was grasping the seat of her chair with both hands, as she backed from me. I need hardly say that I was greatly disturbed in mind and feelings, and forgot all about the origin of the English schools of painters, and the question why the British Museum was more popular than the National Gallery. Thinking that I might have been spattered by a hansom whilst crossing Oxford Street, I passed my hand down my side hastily, with a sense of annoy-' ance, and all at once touched something cold, clammy, that sent a thrill to my heart, and made me start and take a step forward. At the same moment, the lady, with a cry of horror, sprang to her feet, and with raised hands fled from the room, leaving her umbrella where it had fallen. There were other visitors tb the Picture Gallery besides ourselves, who had been passing through the saloon, and they turned at her cry, and looked in surprise after her. The policeman stationed in the room came to me and asked what had happened. I was in such agitation that I hardly knew what to answer. I told him that I could explain what had occurred little better than himself. I had noticed that the lady had worn an odd expression, and had behaved in most extraordinary fashion, and that he had best take charge of her umbrella, and wait for her return to claim it.

This questioning by the official was vexing, as it prevented me from at once and on the spot investi- gating into the cause of her alarm and mine— hers at something she must have seen on my leg, and mine at something I had distinctly felt creep- ing up my leg. The numbing and siekening effect on me of the touch,of the object I had not seen was not to be shaken off at once. Indeed, I felt as though my hand were contaminated, and that I could have no rest till Ihacl thoroughly washed the hand, and, if possthle, washed away the feeling that had been produced- I looktdion the floor, I examined my leg, but saw nothing. As_l wore my overcoat, it was probableethat irvrising from my seat the skirt had fallen over my trousers and hidden the thing, whatever- itAvas. I, therefore, hastily removed my overcoat and shook it, then I looked at my trousers. There was nothing whatever on my leg, and nothing fell from, my overcoat when shaken.

Accordingly, I re-invested myself and hastily left the Gallery; then took my way as speedily as I could, without actually running, to Charing Cross Station and down the narrow way leading to the Metropolitan, where I went into Faulkner's bath ! and hairdressing establishment, and asked for hot water to thoroughly wash my hand and well soap it. I bathed my hand in water as hot as I could endure it, employed carbolic soap, and then, after having a good brush down, especially on my left side where my hand had encountered the object that had so affected me, I left. I had entertained i the intention of going to the Princess's Theatre that evening, and of securing a ticket in the morning; but all thought of theatre-going was gone from me. I could not free my heart from the sense of nausea and cold that liactbeen produced by the touch. I went into Gatti's to have lunch, and ordered something, I forget what,kut when served.
immar

Ercnflippeute was, gone. I could eat nothing my food.inspired ma with disgust. I thrust itdronvme untested, and, after drinking a couple of ,glasses of claret, left the restaurant, and returned'to,my hotel:

Feelinrsick-andtfaint, Pthrewiny overcoat over the sofa back, andkcast-myself on my bed. L do not. know that-there was any particular reason for my doing so, but as Day my eyes were on-my greatcoat. The density of the fog had passed away, and there was light again, not of first quality, but sufficient for a Londoner to swear by, so that I could see-everything in my room, though through a veil, darkly. I do not think my mind was occupied.in any way. About the only occasions on which, to my. know- ledge, my mind is actually passive or inert US when crossing the channel in "The Foata " from Dover to Calais, when I am always, in every weather, abjectly sea-sick—and thoughtless. But as I now lay on my bed, uncomfortable, squeamish, without knowing why—l was in the same inactive mental condition. But riot for long. I saw something that startled me. First, it appeared to me as if the lappet of my overcoat pocket were in movement, being raised. I did not pay much attention to this, as I supposed that the garment was sliding down on to the seat of the sofa, from the back, and that this displace- ment of gravity caused the movement I observed. But this I soon saw was not the case. That which moved the lappet was something in the pocket that was struggling to get out. I -could see now that it was working its way up the inside, and that when it reached the opening it lost balance and fell down again. I could make this out by the pro- jections and indentations in the cloth; these moved as the creature, or whatever it was, worked its way up the lining. "A mouse," I said, and forgot my seediness, I was interested. "The little rascal 1• however did he contrive to seat himself in my pocket, and I have worn that overcoat all the morning I" But no—it was not a mouse. I saw something white poke its way out from under the lappet; and in another moment an object-was revealed that thmigh revealed I could not understand, nor could I dis- tinguish what it was. Now roused by curiosity, I raised myself on my elbow. In doing this I made some noise, the bed creaked. Instantly the something dropped on the floor, lay outstretched for a moment, to recover itself, and then began, with the motions of a maggot to run along the floor. There is a caterpillar called "The Measurer," because when it advances, it draws its tail up to where its head was and then throws forward its full length, and again draws up its extremity, forming at each time a loop; and with each step measuring its total length. The object I now saw on the floor was advancing precisely like the mea- suring caterpillar. It was the colour of a. cheese- maggot, and in length about three and a half inches. It was not, however, like a caterpillar, which is flexible throughout its entire length, but this was, as it seemed to me, jointed in two places, one joint being more conspicuous than the other. For some moments I was so completely paralysed by astonishment, tbat I remained motionless, looking at the thing as it crawled along the carpet, a dull green carpet with darker green, almost black, flowers in it. _ _ _

It had, as it seemed tome, a glossy head, dis- tinctly marked; but as the light was not brilliant, I could not make out very clearly, and, moreover, the rapid movements prevented close scrutiny. Presently, with a shock still more startling than that' produced by its apparition at the opening of the pocket of my great-coat, I became convinced that what I saw was a finger, a human forefinger, and that the glossy hes 4 was nothing other than the nail.

It did not seem to have been amputated. There was no sign of blood or laceration where the knuckle should be but the extremity of the finger, or root rather, faded away to indistinctness, and I was as unable to make out that end of the finger as I was the point. I could see no hand, no body behind this finger, nothing whatever except a finger that had little token of life in it, no coloration as though blood circu- lated in- -it-;'-and this -finger was in active motion ci tepliig along the carpet towards kwardrobe that steud .gairist the wall by the fireplace. I Pp; ~ng out of bed and pursued it. E ~,undy the finger was alarmed, but it re- dool, e,i ;is oacu, reached the wardrobe and went under ii,. iiy the time I bad arrived at the article of furniture it hail disappeared. I lit a vesta niateit and held it beneath the wardrobe that was raiud ahuve the cagpet by about two inches, on turned feet, but I coidd see nothing more of the finger. got my umbrella and thrust it beneath, and raker.' 'forwards and backwards, right and left, and raked out flue; and nothing more -solid.

I packed my portmanteau next day and returned to my home in the country. All desire for amuse- ment in town was gone, and the faculty to transact business had departed as well. A languor and qualms had come over me, and my heal.' was in a maze. I was unable to fa my thoughtwn anything. At times I was disposed to belim74; that my wits were deserting me, at others that I was on the verge of a severe illness. Anyhow, whether likely to go off my head or not, or take.to my bed, home was the only place for me, and homeward I sped, accordingly. On reach- ing my country habitation, my servant, as usual took my pormauteau to my bedroom unstrapped it, but did not unpack it. I object to his throwing out the contents of my Gladstone bag; not that there is anything in it he may not see, but that he puts my things where I cannot find them again. My clothes—he is welcome to place them where he likes and where they belong, and this latter he knows better than I do; but, then, I carry about with me other things than a dress suit, and changes of linen and flannel. There are letters, papers, books—and the proper destinations of these is known only to myself. A servant has a singular and evil knack of putting away literary matter and odd volumes in such places that it takes the owner half a day to find them again. Although I was uncomfortable' and my head in a whirl, I opened and unpacked my own pormanteau. As I was thus engaged I saw sometlfing curled up. in my collar box, the lid of which had got broken in, by a boot-heel infringing on it. I had pulled off the damaged cover to see if my collars had been spoiled, when something curled up inside suddenly rose on end and leapt, just like a cheese-jumper, out of the box, over the edge of the Gladstone bag, and scurried away across the floor in a manner already familiar to me. I could not doubt for a moment what it was— here was the finger again. It had come with me from London to the country. Whither it went in its run over the floor I do not know, I was too bewildered to observe.

Somewhat later, towards evening, I seated myself in my easy chair, took up a book and tried to read. I was tired with the journey, with the knocking about in town, and the discomfort and alarm produced by the apparition, of the finger. I felt worn out. I was unable to give my attention tolwhat I read, and before I was aware was asleep. Roused for an instant by the fall of the book from my hands, I speedily relapsed into unconscious- ness. lam not sure that a doze in an arm-chair ever does good. It usually leaves me in a semi- stupid condition and with a headache. Five minutes in a•horizontal position on my bed is worth thirty in a chair. That is my experience. In sleeping in a sedentary position the head is a diffi- culty, it drops forward or lolls on one side or the other, and has to be brought back into a position in which the line to the centre of gravity runs through the trunk, otherwise the head carries the body over in a sort of general capsize out of the chair on to the floor.

Now I slept, on the occasion lam speaking of, pretty healthily, because deadly weary; but I was brought to waking, not by my head falling over the arm of the chair, ant my trunk tumbling after it, but by a feeling of cold extending from my throat to my heart. When I awoke I was in a diagonal nosition. with my riaht ear reEtinz

shoulder, and exposing the left side of my throat, and it was here—where the jugular vein throbs— that I felt the greatest intensity of cold. At once I shrugged my left shoulder, rubbing my neck with the collar of my coat in so doing. Immediately something fell off, upon the floor„ and I again saw the finger. My disgust—horror, were intensified when I perceived that it was dragging something after it, which might have been an old stocking, and which I took at first glance for something of the sort. The evening sun shone in through my window, in a brilliant golden ray that lighted the object as it tumbled along. With this illumination I was able to distinguish what the object was. It is not easy to describe it, but I will make the attempt. The finger I saw Wlie solid and material; what it drew after it was neither, or was only in a nebu- lous proto-plasinic condition. The finger was attplhed to a hand which was curdling into matter and in process of acquiring solidity r attached to the hand was an arm in a very filmy condition, and this arm belonged to a human body in a still more vaporous, immaterial condition. This was being dragged along the floor by the finger, just as a silk- worm might pull after it the tangle of its web. I could see legs and arms, and head, and coat-tail tumbling about and interlacing and disentangling again in a promiscuous manner. There was no bone, no, muscle, no substance in the figure; the members were attached to the trunk which was spineless, but they had evidently no functions, and were • wholly dependent on the finger which pulled them along in a jumble of parts as it advanced. In such confus.on did the whole vaporous matter seem, that I think—l cannot say for certain it was so, but the impreSs.on left on my mind was—that one of the eyeballs was looking out at a nostril, and the tongue lo ling out of one of the ears. It was, however, only for a moment that I saw this germ-body; I cannot call by another name that which had not more substance than smoke. I saw it only so long as it was being dragged athwart the ray of sunlight. The moment it was pulled jerkily out of the beam into the shadow beyond, I could see nothing of it, only the crawling finger. I had not sufficient moral energy, or physical force in me to rise, pursue, and stamp on the finger, and grind it with my heel into the floor. Both seemed drained out of me. What became of the finger, whither it went, how it managed to secrete itself, Ido not know. I had lost the power to enquire. I sat in my chair, chilled, staring before me into space. "Please, sir," a voice said, "There's Mr. Square below, electrical engineer." "Eli?" I looked dreamily round. My valet was at the door. "Please, sir! The gentleman would be glad to be allowed to go over the house and see that all the electrical apparatus is in order." "Oh, indeed! Yes—show him up." (To be concluded.)

A bookmaker appeared before bis Honour Judge Cad- man, at Halifax County Court, on Tuesday, on a judg- ment summons. This year, he pleaded, bookmakers had had a very bad time, and he also urged his Honour to remember that winter was coming on. His }amour : Yes, but there is steeplechasing, isn't there ? div.p: TRADES THAT K!LL.
Painters' Colic at Blackburn.

Among the many employments which sooner or - later cause acute suffering to those who follow them may belmentioned the match makers' trade, which in duces the terrible malady known as " pilaus'-jaw "-- the white lead industry, which has wrecked the lives of thousands of men and women ; also the telegraph oprrators' calling, which often causes a peculiar and obstinate nervous affectioN, But perhaps the common- est trade disease to which Blackburn is subject, is painters' colic. The men who have experienced the severe paroxysmal pains of the last mentioned malady will value any advice that may enable there to avoid a repetition of them. Some hints to this end were recently given to a reprreentative of the' Blackburn Standard and Express" by a well-known Blackburn master-painter, Mr William Pickup.

I speak from a long I experience of the trade, as I am a master painter of some years' standing, whilst my father is one of the , oldest master-painters in the town. The pills have done so much for me that I would not be without them at any price. They have saved me pounds." "International Arbitration." This was the subject of a lecture delivered by Mt Mark Howarth, of the Liverpool Peace Society, before the members of the Wycliffe Young People's Society at a meeting held in the Memorial Build. iegs on Monday evening. International arbitration. he said really meant a code of laws that was agreed upon by civilised nations. This was not a new subject. The Greeks and Romans made use of arbitration in the settlement of dieputes. In later years the ices of international arbitration had found more general aceeptance,and there were over 300 distinct cases where international arbitration had settled disputes. In referring to the continual growth of armaments due to the spirit of militarism, no said more than two-thirds of every sovereign paid in taxes went towards the mainten- ance of the army and navy. Could not we settle our disputes with foreign nations in a more rational manner than by an appeal to arms? thought we could, and a seep In the right directlon was the insertion of arbitral clauses in treaties between nations. which stipulated that in Case Of disagreement, arbitration should be resorted to. Reference was made to the action of the Czar of Russia which led to the conference at the Hague. He believed the Czar was sincere in his desire for the establishment of a permanent court of arbitra- tion which could be resort,d to by any nation in case of dispute. Reference was also made to the necessity of a common understanding among the nations of the world for an arrest of armaments.— An interesting discussion followed, taken part in by the chairman (Mr W Brown), Mr William Bee- wick, Mr W Booth, Mr J Gauld, Mr J Wallington I and Mr J Ball.—The passing of the usual votes of I thanks terminated a pleasant and profitable evening.

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK
ROYAL _TORS HIM AND H.M. THE

During next week and the week after England will be visited by two European rulers, who are coming over to stay with his Majesty to con- gratulate him upon his recovery from his illness. These two sovereigns are his nephews, the Kaiser and his great personal friend, the King of Portugal: and their visits will immediately succeed each other. The Kaiser is due to arrive on Saturday at Port Victoria in the Holten:ollern, and will pro- ceed at once to Shorncliffe, where he will review the Ist Royal Dragoons, of which he is)aOnorary colonel, and present them with their war-medals. The parade will be a khaki one, and the men will show themselves off to their Imperial colonel in the kit they have worn at the front. The Kaiser will be the guest of Lieut.-Colonel Lord Basing, who was gazetted a Commander of the Bath last Friday in recognition of his services at the front, during his short visit to Shorncliffe : and the Royals will beg his acceptance of the wildbeeste they brought home from the veldt, which was first falsely reported to be a gift for King Edward. Upon the same day the Kaiser will travel with his suite to Sandringham to be in time for the celebrations of the King's birthday on the 9th: and during the early days of next week he will shoot over the Sandringham covers, which are some of the best in the KingdOm. On Friday he will travel north with his suite to stay with Lord ronsdale at Lowther Castle, where he has previously visited the Earl. Upon leaving Lowther Castle the Kaiser will proceed straight home; rejoining the lichen, zollern probably at Leith. The visit of the King of Portugal will follow immediately upon the heels of the German Emperor's, as he is due to arrive at Windsor Castle upon the 17th inst. He left Portugal upon the 15th of last month, and has since then been staying in Paris incognito in com- pany with the Maquitt de Soveral, King Edward's great friend. The Queen of Portugal hasl in the meantime, been .appointed Regent during her Consort's absence. It is uncertain whether the visit of King Carlos has any political significance as, if so, this side of the question is being kept very dark: but the Continental papers are con- vinced that it has as its ntiiif Anglo-Portuguese relations in Africa and the Delagoa Bay question. But it is more probable that it, like the Kaiser's, is purely a friendly visit, and it will be /equally private in character and free from ceremony, as King Edward and King Carlos are the closest of personal friends. The King of Portugal will shoot over the Windsor preserve's and is expected to do great execution as he is one of the crack shots of Europe. His visit will probably con- clude upon the 24th inst., when he will return ,to Paris. One of the last of the Coronation ceremonies, which took place during his Majesty's recent stay in town was the presentation of a Bible in com- memonition of the Coronation under the auspices of the British and Foreign Bible Society, in which the royal family have always shown such an interest. The presentation was made at Buckingham Palace by the Marquis of North- ampton, accompanied by the Archbishop of: Canterbury, the Revd. Principal Fairbairn, of Mansfield College, Oxford, Mr. Caleb Kemp, chairman of the committee, and the Revd. J. H. Ritson, the secretary. The Marquis made a short speech, concluding : " We humbly ask your Majesty to accept this copy of the inspired Word of God, and we are proud to know that it will remain in the possession of your Majesty and your Majesty's descendants as a memorial of your

div.head: AFRICA.
div.p: AFRICA.

and the action of a true statesman : and from this voyage the outcome can only be good. u means that Mr. Chamberlain wishes to obtain first-hand information on the situation before coming to any final conclusions as to taxation, allowances, mode of settlement and the thousand and one minor questions with which ,the South African problem bristles; and it proves that he does not flinch from taking upon his own shoulders the whole onus of th , final resettlement of affairs to vay nothing of personal risks which he must undoubtedly run. In view of his position as a Cabinet Minister, and the importance of his mission, it was only meetthat a war- ship should be placed at his disposal; and this gra- cious act on the part al King Edward has been widely

approved, and no happier selection could have been made than the first-class cruiser Good Hope, which was so named out of compliment to Cape Colony, and is paid for by their grant of £30,000 a year. to the Navy. The date of Mr. Chamberlain's departure has beeen fixed for Saturday, the 15th, when he will join the Good Hope at Portsmouth. Arrange- ments are on foot in Birmingham to entertain the Colonial Secretary at a monster non-political banquet on the evening preceding his departure: and many eminent people hope to be present at this pleasant function. There is no doubt that by his decision Mr. Chamberlain has won himself a position he never held efore in the public estimation: and no previous action in his strenuous and combative political life has given such satis- faction to all parties and shades of opinion. Two soldiers who have recently been brought into public notice are Generals Oliphant and Manning. The former, Major-General Laurence Oliphant, who was gazetted a C.B. for his services in South Africa last Friday, has been appointed to the command of the 9th (Foot Guards) Brigade of the 2nd Army Corps, and to succeed Sir Henry
M.V.0., APPOINTED TO THE COMMAND OF THE
HOME' DISTRICT, AND BRIGADIER-GENERAL
MANNING, IN COMMAND AT THE BASE OF THE
SOMALILAND EXPEDITION.

Trotter in command of the Home District, a highly important post which that general vacates at the end of the present year after a record term of royal pageants successfully managed. General Oliphant, who is fifty-five years of age, was appointed to the command of an infantry brigade at Aldershot in February, 1900, and subsequently went to South Africa, where he was lately in command of the Elan'ds- fontein District and Klerksdorp Sub-District. In 1895 he served in the Soudan, receiving the medal and Suakin clasp and the bronze star. Brigadier-General Manning, who commands the East African Protectorate, is an Indian Staff Corps officer, who has seen considerable service; and at present he is placed in a very anxious position, being in charge of the reinforcements to be sent up to Colonel Swayne, who has reached Berbera safely. The last-named officer will, according to present plans, remain in charge of the active part of the expedition against the Mullah, retaining supreme command in the field, while General Manning will be in command at the base. Col. Swayne's present force, which only consists of 860 properly disciplined black troops and 1,500 local levies, is being reinforced by 1,700 Indian troops and a thousand men of the King's African Rifles, with guns and transport.

The last sessions at the Old Bailey have just been brought to a close; and this historic court, which has for, so many years been the centre of British criminal trials, will, under the scheme of the demolition of Newgate, shortly cease to exist. The name "Old Bailey" has often mistakenly been confused with " baillie " and " "•; but its real origin lies in the medimval Latin word "balliunt," which meant the space within castle or City walls, and in this case referred to the portion of the City walls between Newgate and Ludgate. In Durham and other parts of England, also, the word" bailey "is found with the simple significance of a street. Many volumes might be written round the various famous trials which have taken place at the Old Bailey or Central Criminal Court, as it has of teii been called in modern times, ag not only has practically every famous criminal within

JIONS AT TILE OLD BAILEY. the neighbourhood of the metropolis been tried there, but also many from all parts of the country, when there was any fear of local prejudice, as. for instance, in the case of Palmer, the Rugeley poisoner, and quite recently in the case of Bennett, the Yarmouth murderer. Crimes of all kinds from treason to petty larceny, came within the jurisdiction of this great central court : and only of late years comparatively has the extension of quarter sessions lightened its calendar. Amongst the most historic cases tried at the Old Bailey may be mentioned those of the surviving judges of King Charles I. in 1660 immediately after the Restora- : the patriotic Lord William Russell in 1683: Jack Sheppard in 1724: Jonathan Wild a year later the poet Savage in 1727: the infamous Dr. Dodd a half a century after : Bollingham, who assassinated the statesman Percival in the lobby of the House of Commons, in 1812: the Cato Street conspirators in 1820 : and murderers, forgers, genus mune, galore. But now it has closed its historic doors, and London's criminals will no Longer have their due meted out to them in the same spot, whence so -many thousand of their predecessors have been led off to execution, trans- portation and lighter penalties proportionate to their crimes. But, however much may be lost in historic association, as much will be gained in convenience and ventilation, as the Old Bailey has always been notorious for its lack of accommodation and fresh air,
MAJOR-GENERAL LAWRENCE OLIPHANT, C,13.,

div.head: Compensation Claim Settled.
div.p: Compensation Claim Settled.

At the Warrington County Court. on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, Elizabeth Beckett, of Heatley Heath, near VVarringcon, was the applicant in-a claim under the Workmen's Compensation Act for £l5l 183 10d from the Cheshire Lines Committee, for the maintenance of herself and children in her bereavement. The applicant's late husband win a, shunter in the em- ploy of the Cheshire Lines Committee. and whilst en- gaged in shunting operations on the let of September last, at the railway siding in Battersby-lane, he was knocked down and injured by a light engine. He sus- tained a broken leg, three broken ribs and an injury to the head. He died at the Infirmary on the 4th September. Mr Browne, who appeate3 for the applicant, said the Cheshire Lines Committee had been represented by Messrs Lingards, solicitors, Manchester, and they bad paid the full amount into court. Mr Lingard was us- able to be present in Court, but he admitted the amount was due, and the only question to be decided was what was to be done with the money. The applicant was a widow, and there were five children living at the time the application was filed. Since then another ckild had been born, and therefore there were six children to be provided for. Ile (Mr Browne) suggested, and it met with the approval of all parties, that Mr James Collins, the widow's father, and himself (Mr Browne) should be trustees and that the money should he invested in their joint names, with power to pay the widow whatever amounts per week were considered reasonable. Mr Collins was a most respectable man and was a platelayer on the London and North-Western Railway Company for was also trustee for another married daughter. The respondents were quite prepared to leave the matter in His Honour's bands. His Honour asked what the trustees intended to

—.„ Mr Browne said the applicant had already drawn £5O from an accident fund so that she bad that sum to be going on with. There was no immediate need for assistance and it was not intended to touch the present sum until the money in band was exhausted. They in- tended to invest the money and pay out of capital and interest any reasonable weekly sum for the support of the applicant and six children, until the money was ex- hausted. His Honour agreed with this nourso being taken and made an order for the money to be paid to Mr Arthur Browne and Mr James Collins. to be used for the main- tenance of the applicant and children in their bereave- ment. He allowed the applicant's costs in the action, subject to notice being given to the respondents.

div.head: WARRINGION BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGION BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held in the Board Room at the Work- house on Wednesday morning. Dr Patterson presided and there were also present :—Mrs Clay, Rev T R Matthews. Rev Father Wilson, Messrs A Brooks, A J Jolley, A Jolley, G Pilling, J Billinge, T H Ashcroft, J Payton, J Clarke, R Forshaw, E L Bent, T Halton, T Ritchie, J Tinton, W Houghton, G Mather, with J C Sutton (clerk), S Sutton (assistant clerk), F Gate (master), A Wright (superintendent Padgate Schools).

_ THE DIFFICULTY WITH PROBATIONER NURSES. The House Committee reported that the offer of the Borough Electrical Engineer to test the new work by Messrs Morton and Company had been accepted, and that reasonable charges be paid to the engineer for the work. The Committee recommended that the night porter's salary be increased from 25s to Hs per week. It was further recommended that Mrs Kate Carter be appointed laundress to succeed Mrs Tudor, resigned at a salary of £2B per annum ;that the laundry accommodation be increased by an extension of existing buildings and that Messrs Owen be instructed to prepare detail plans, specifications and estimates for proposed extensions and consequent structural altera- tions. The Matron was asked to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Miss Delahay. The resignation was also reported of Miss Miner as probationer nurse. It wars recommended that Miss A Read be appointed prebstioner nurse at a salary of £1.2 for the first year, £l6 for the next year, and £2O for the third year. The CLERK, alluding to the changes with reference to the probationer nurses, said a great number of answers to questions bad to be sent to the Local Government Board before receiving the confirmation of the appoint- ment of any of the nurses. Three had resigned, thus producing a state of things which was very perplexing as well as troublesome. He should like the Chairman of the committee to explain how these difficulties arose. After the nurses bad left lie would receive from the Local Government Board confirmation of their appoint- ments. (Laughter). Mr BREVES, in reply. said it was vita as perplexing and confusing to the House C)mmittee as to the Clerk to ' the Guardians. The real reason seemed to be that there was no resident medical officer or system of lectures whereby the probationers might learn the theoretical part of their duties as wallas the practical part. It was a question whether the House Committee or the Board should arrange for lectures to be given to the proba- tioners and nursen. Tnat was a matter for considera- tion. (Hear, hear). Mr PILLING seconded, and the minut 19 were passed.

LIFE WRECKED BY INDIGESTION.
Confined Indoors for Nine Years.

div.head: Debility and Rheumatism Ensued.
div.p: Debility and Rheumatism Ensued.
Bile Beans Restored Health.

Miracles are said not to occur now-a-days, but this case—proved, vouched for, by neighbours, reads very like one. Mrs Susan Harkness, to subject,lives at 76i. Kirk-street, Calton, Glasgow. and here is her story : " For nine long years prior to last February I was not able to go out of my house ! This was due to various illneises and ailments but right down at the bottom of them all, and causing them all, was chronic indigestion , This weakened and debilitated my whole system and 1 various evils resulted. My boy there has just turned nine, and about a week afrsr he was born I began to have terrible pains in my back and °hest. I could not digest what food I took, was sick, weak and dizzy, and it really seemed actual torture for me to drag myself about. Housework was out of eht, question.

Then bilious attacks began to come on and day after day I would be in a condition of utter helplessness. I was unable to sleep at night, but often during the day a kind of stupor would creep over me. Added to my pain from these various ailments I then began to suffer from rheumatism. Once the body gets run down it is really surprising how many ills steal in ! For years I suffered. At times I was under doctor's treatment, and from one medical man I had sixteen bottles of medicine without getting any benefit. Things went on in this way until [tried Chas. Forde's Bile Beans. div.head: LOCAL NEWS
div.p: LOCAL NEWS
The Police Court and Prison Gate Mission

The following is a summary of the work of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Liver- pool Diocesan C.E.T.S. for the month of October 258 visits were made to 26 police and petty sessional courts in Liverpool, Warrington, St. Helens, Prescot, Newton-le-Willows and South West Lancashire. In the course of these visits the I members of the staff conversed with 1431 parsons in the courts and bridewells of whom 727 were subsequently visited in their bodes. Eighty-five women and girls, and 75 lads were provided with employment, taken to homes sr restored to relations and friends. Two other women were taken to the Society's Temperance Home. 139 persons ware attende Ito in the courts at the request of the magistrates, and 109 were desired to do so by the Court officials and the police. Iu eight instances the loss of employment was averted through the efforts of the Missionaries. In 39 instances clothing was provided to enable the recipients to accept employment. 36 cases were handed over to the clergy and ministers of religion tor future over sight. At the Mission Room near Walton prison- which is open daily, 674 persons were provided with breakfast on discliaage from the jail, and offers of work, and help were made to all. 82 per- sons were visited in theirabodes from the prisons. 58 tickets for work at the Society's Fire- wood and Mat Factory, Bootle were given to men, 302 letters were written with reference to persons being helped. An aggregate of 291 men, women and young persons visited the office; and the homes of the Missionaries to be assisted. In 149 instances parents and friends of persons who were in danger of committing offences or crime sought and obtained the advice and co- operation ot the Missionaries, 155 persons were spoken to in lodging houses 49 men were conversed with on trans and bus stands, 309 total abstinence ! pledges were ad ministered,ss meetings addressed &c
THE NORTHERN RUGBY LEAGUE.
First Division. WARRINGTO3 LOSE AT HULL.

Warrington took a full te sm to Hull on Saturday last and as the hemesters were without Taylor,the County full back,they felt pretty confident ofiannexing two points at the expanse of the sea-porters. Hull. however, played a strong forward game, end a few minuteeirom the close of play scored the winning points. The special train from Warrington took a good number of spectators. Mr Bunckshaw. of Stockport, was the referee, and the teams lined out in the following order before 8,00 people. Hull—Jacques, 7ack ; R W Jackson, Cook, Morgan, and Parry, three-quarter backs ; Hall and Goddard, half backs; Lewis, Miller,Wade, Speneeleyalarmer, Harrison,Langhorn. and Parkiason. forwards. Warrington—T Knight. back ; Fish, Dickenson, Isherwood and Harris, three-quarter backs ; Burgess and Hockenhall, halt backs; Morrison, Boardman, W Swif t,F Swift, Edmond- son. Forster, Roberts, and Taylor, forwards. Soon after the commencement Warrington were penalized and Jacques placed a goal. This spurred the visitors to greater exertions. Warrington had been doing some smart and tricky work in the passing game, and by this means Isherwood sc,red a pretty try without meeting very serious opposition, and Fish had no difficulty in adding the goal. Before the interval Morgan scored, but Jacques failed at goal, so the teams had live points each--There was a slackening after the change, and play lacked interest for some time. Warrington, however, made a splendid defence, and seemed ts be invincible Fish, who was frequently conspicuous, did good service for his side, and till within a few minutes of the close a drawn game seemed certiin, when Jackson, who was on the " 25" line, getting hold of the ball after a pass from Goddard, beat all comers for spied and scored a try, giviag his side the victory. Jacques a(ain Lane lat goal. Result : Hull. 1 goal and 2 tries (8 points) ; Warrington. I goal and 1 try (5 points), HALIFAX v ST. HELENS.

The meeting of these teams drew about 6,003 spectators to the Haneon-lane Ground. Halifax early on got into the visitors' quarters, but the visitors by means of kicks from marks and penalties kept Halifax on the defensive for some time. Their backs relied upon kicking into touch, and seldom tried to break through to the line. though Liversedge was near scoring on one occasion. The Halifax forwards did much better after this, and their backs were several times in possession. Two or three good combined movements followed, in which the two half backs, and Williams. Hod- man, and Joe Riley took a prominent part, but when half- time arrived neither side had scored—Halifax in the second half had a decided advantage. The first score resulted from a rush by the forwards, who went over the line In a body. Sumrnerskill grounding the ball. Hadwen kicked a goal from the place. The backs had the credit for the second try. Williams got the ball alter it had passed through the hands of Nettleton and Brown, and scored with a brilliant run. Wedgewood failed at goal, St Helens afterwards lost the services of Lea, who was ordered off by the referee. Result :—Halifax 1 goal. 2 tries (8 points), St Helens nil. Teams : Halifax : Jones. back : Wedgewood, Joe Riley, Williams, and Hadwen, three-quarter backs; Nettleton and Brown, half basks; DickensonMammond, Morton, Wilson, Buttner, I Surnmerskill, Swinbank, and Longbottom, forwards. St. Helens : Lambert, back ; Liversidge. Doherty. B Creevey, and J Creevey, three•quarter backs ; Hall and Banks, half backs; Carnev, Thompson. Green, Lea, Mooney, Mamma, Prescott, and Whiteley. forwards. Referee. Mr F Hancock. Runcorn. Touch judges, Mr T H Marshall (Bradford), and Mr 71' II Shaw (Batley).

div.head: SALFORD v. RUNCORN.
div.p: SALFORD v. RUNCORN.

This fixture took place at the Willows, Weaste. before 7,000 spectators Farmer started for Runcorn, who were first to attack, Jolley being prominent. Play was transferred to the (entre, after which Salford made a strong forward burst, and Tunney passing to Bell. he ran over behind the poste. From an easy place Griffiths landed a goal. Succeeding play was in favour of the "reds." who repeatedly gained a lot of I ground. and it was only effeetive tackling by Honghten and Jolley that kept Riley and Bell from scoring. Occasionally the visitors' three-quarters secured possession, and good work by Dutton and Price resulted in the lest-named get- ting over at the far corner. Farmer failed at the place. Just before the interval Jones gave Runcorn the lead with a well-deserved try, which Jolley I failed to improve. Half-time score :—Runcorn. 2 tries (6 points) ; Salford, 1 goal and 1 try (5 points). I On resuming play was of an evea character for a time until Rodgers got poesession and had practically a clear run to the line, but failed to elude Houghton. Riley and Bell several times nearly got over, but the Runcorn defence pre- vailed until within a minute of the finish, when Oriffiths fed Riley from a scrummage, and Bell eventually getting possession ran over at the corner. Brown kicked a goal from the place. Result :—Salford. 2 goals 2 tries (10 points) ; Runcorn. 2 tries (6 points). Teams r Salford—D Davies, back; lodgers, Riley, Bell and Norris, three-quarter backs ; Harter and Griffiths, half backs : Rhapps, Williams, Tunney, Heath, Brown, R Shaw, T Shaw, and Shore forwards. _ .

Ruaeorn—Honghton, balk ; Jones, Warder. Dutton and Price, three-quarter backs ; Richardson and Jolley, half backs ; Walker, Farmer, Woods, Higgins, Moulton. Gayter. Williams, and Tomlinson, forwards. Referee, W McCutcheon, Oldham ; touch judges, It , Leigh and W Oakes, Werneth. WIDNES v. HULL KINGSTON BOVEES.

. _ Played at Widnes before 2,030 spectators. Widnes won the toss, and had the advantage of a strong wind. They attacked strongly, and Peacock and Ike Taylor were pulled dawn a few yards from the line. The Hull ba,f backs, by judielous kicking, gradually removed the danger. Widnes, however, returned to the attack, and when in a good position Hall were penalised. Aspey attempted to place a goal, but the ball fell short. 'remade amends, however, a few minutes later by placing a god. There was nothing more ecored,sitid on turning round the Chemicals led by 2 points to nil. Zarly on in the Second half the home backs played in greatly improved form, and for a time the Hull defence was sorely taxed. Theo Lally made an opening. and passed to Brawn, who passed to Peacock, and the latter scored behind the pests. Tilley improved. After this Widnes had matters all their owa way. Just before the whistle blew Tilley placed a goal from a mark. Result :--Widnes 3 goals I try (9 points), Hull Kingston Rovers nil. Teams : Widnes— Tilley, back ; Hughes, Brown, I Taylor. and Pea— cock, three quarters ; A Taylor and Lally,half hicks ; Aspey, Power. aurtis. Webster, Riley, Rigby, Lynch, and Leysbon, forwards.

Hull Kingston Rovers —Sinclair, back ; West, Gordon, Chant, and Idadeley, three-quarters ; Goth and Garde, half backs ; Lewis. Walker. Pickering. Taylor, Townsley, Windle. Gorman, and Cole, for wards. Referee, F Clegg (Wfanningham) ; touch judges, F Turner (Warrington), and W Jones (Runcorn).

div.head: OLDHAM V HUDDERSFIELD.
div.p: OLDHAM V HUDDERSFIELD.

These teams met at Watersheddings, before a small attend- Soc. Before the game had been in progress three minutes Spottiswcode had scored a try as the result of a pass from Lees. Deere, Dewhirst and Kitchen made very deter- mined attempts to equalise, but when the interval arrived Oldham was leading ,y a try to nil. Huddersfield restarted and the first inci.letat of note that transpired was a grand run by Deere, after a smart exhibition of passing on the part of the backs, which almost resulted in a score R Thomas just managing to kiek the ball dead. Oldham again came to the front, and P Thomas and Soottiswoode were both nearly over. About five minutes off " time " Spottiswoode was successful in penetrating the defence, but Ferguson failed to improve. Result —Oldham, 2 tries (6 points) ; Hudders- field, nil.

div.head: LEIGH V BRIGHJUSE _RANGEROI.
div.p: LEIGH V BRIGHJUSE _RANGEROI.

Played at Leigh before nearly MOO spectators. At the interval Brighouse led by a frost to nothint,•,—Leigh went off with a great burst In the second half, and Brighouse had to concede two penalties in quick succession. Play was of a scrambling character. At last, from near the centre, John- son placed a penalty goal for Leigh. Brighouse attaaked strongly after this, and twice narrowly missed scoring. Leigh raised the siege, and by long kicking took play to the Brig-
house quarter, where passing by Boardman, Kirk, and Mars, ended in Roberts souring. Johnson failed at goal. Result : Leigh, 1 goal and 1 try (5 points) ; Brighouse Rangers, 1 goal (2 points).

WIGAN V. HUNSLET. These teams met at Central Park, Wigan, where there was a large attendance In the opening half the home team were seen to advantage, tbe backs playing very effectivsly, and the Hunslet line was repeatedly in danger. largely owing to bungling on the part of the three-quar te x and a weak die. play by Farrar at full back. It was, however, well on in the half before Rothwell placed Wigan ahead by a finely kicked goal. In the secend half Hunslet had several excellent chances of not only equalising,but of gaining a commanding position. Feebleness of support to the fine work of the forwards, and the inability of A Goldthorpe to realise points from splendid positions acnunted for the defeat of the visitors. Result : Wiganl goal (2 points), Hunslet nil.

- BRADFORD V BROUGHTON RINGERS. There were about 6,000 spectators present at this match at Bradford. Bradford were short of five men, on duty for the County. and were thus heavily handicapped. Losing the toss, Whitehead kicked off for Broughton in the direction of the city. The opening was tame, but shortly after Widdeson got over from a pass by Hogg, W James failing to kick the easiest of goals, Mosby had three or four shots at goal from penalties and marks, most of which he should have kicked. The change of ends came with Broughton 3 points ahead. For the first moiety of the second half Bradford made very strong running, Burman and Brear. the half backs, play- ing well. Wilson dropped a very fine goal for Bronghton, and later. Mosby having a kick charged. Widdeson scored a good try, W James failing to kick the goal. Result Broughton Rangers, Rangers, 1 goal and 1 tries (8 points) ; Bradford, nil.

SWINTON V. BATLEY. Five thousand spectators were present at this match on the Swinton ground. The game bad not been in progress many minutes before liampson scored after a grand run by R Valentine. No goal resulted, and then Auty had his kick charged down, with the result that Cborley picked up and scored a soft try. Preston placed a goal, and repeated the feat shortly afterwards when Waliwork put on a third try. Batley had a turn at pressing, thanks to admirable foot work by the forwards, but try as they would the visitors could make no Impression on the home defense. Nothing further transpired up to the interval, when the score stood—Swinton 2 goals and 3 tries (13 points), Batley nil. On resuming Swinton immediately attacked, but the defence defied all attempts at penetration. Roebuck stopped Hampson in fine style, and theta, thanks to Goodall, the home team were forced to defend Hot work ensued on the Swinton line, and D Fitzgerald ultimately placed a penalty goal. Subsequently they had hard lines, Oborley on one occasion only just managing to make the bail dead. Valentine at length relieved and Ryan@ put on another try for Swinton, Preston placing a goal. Result :—Swinton 3 goals and 4 tries (18 points) Batley 1 goal (2 points.)
