div.head: EXAMINER. NOVEMBER 7th, 1902.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. NOVEMBER 7th, 1902.

IN the speech made by The Liberal Leaders oIR 0 HENRY CAMPBELL- and Liberal Unity. BANNERMAN at the Alexandra Palace, London, on Saturday,to a meet- ing variously estimated to contain from 11,000 to 118' 000 persons, there was what may I be regarded as a friendly message to LORD ROSEBERY, who had I his own great meeting at Edinburgh on the same evening. The pressing necessity of the time iø the opinion of the Liberal leader in the House of Commons is a Government that will redress the injustice that the existing G overnment is seeking to impose. "I do not care who are the men who will compose it," he observed, thus indicating his own readiness to stand aside should circumstances seem to make that step advisible iti the interests of Liberal unity. The reunific- ation of the Liberal party, however, is t° be sought not through this mole of self- sacrifice, but by the bringing together iu friendly alliance for a common purpose of those who are its natural chiefs. Turning to Lord I ROSEBERY'S Edinburgh speech, we find nothing that does .not tend towards the removal of ditfi- I culties, which are the reanit rather of misunder- standing than of differences of principle. To Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN'S suggestion of 5 ' meeting of the leaders Lord ROSEBERY responds frankly and at once by heartily welcoming the proposal. For his part he says he will do all that 1 in him lies to promote the carrying-out of the suggestion, and will urge this friends to do the same. The object of such a conference he states with admirable conciseness and clearness. It should be to promote a common campaign against the Conservative Government. That is, of course, the work that lies nearest to the hand of the Liberal party. It is for the leaders to place themselves in such relations to each other as will inspire public confidence in thou as anternative to the existing administration. party with divided counsels is not a party that could hope to successfully face the polls. But is the party really so divided as it seems ? Is there even so much difference of view between some tif the leaders as it has lately been the fashion to be- lieve ? The explanation given by Lord RosEassif on Saturday of the meaning of certain phrases which have played a not very fortunate part in Liberal speeches of late, makes agreement 110° merely possible, but should bring it near. Stand' ing by itself the advice to clean the Liberal slat° looks like an invitation to abandon well-ostablishe4 principles; but explained as Lord ROSEBERY er plained it at Edinburgh on Saturday as a policy 1:4 adaptation to the political demands of the hour, without any cutting away of the work which tbs Liberal party is pledged to accomplish, it becomes altogether practical and praiseworthy. Tne quer tion of what is to he done first must, it is clear, b° decided by circumstances when the Liberal part/ returns to power. Whoever may be its leaders,thet work will be first undertaken which is most dir_, tinctly crying out to be done. The Libore'i programme, says Lord ROSEBERY, should be suite° to the time; and as he immediately went on ta 1 I show he is not, in saying this, pleading for a Mere 'policy of expediency. He is thinking of what will Ibe the condition of national and imperial affair when his MAJESTY'S present Minister l are over:a 4 thrown. He does not suggest that the Liher ~.., 1 s party should turn its back on the questions ' which it has been accustomed to deal in the 04' There will be general satisfaction among Liberaisi with his clear repudiation of a policy ° '0 "cleaning the slate" in and such sense as thl9. Lord ROSEBERY'S precise declarations on this sub' ject make the Edinburgh speech the most import- ant step toward Liberal reunion that has yet been made. :So much being clear, no divergence of v,ilic! can arise over the demand for efficiency. v" v are all of us in favour of efficient administrations
I
B:
fly tea to ere lire rich ist• of vs• rt üb- eon iew We on,
I

and we are all disposed to agree with Lord ROSE- BERY that this question is for the time being more important than any other. The plac- ing of the affairs of the nation and the Empire on a business footing is a work that calls out sorely to be done; and, so far from shrinking from that great task, the Liberal party is eager for its opportunity. The word "efficiency" should be a rallying cry, not a cause of dissension, and certainly Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN will stand shoulder to shoulder with Lord ROSEBERY in relation to that part of his programme. Liberals will welcome, too, the improved tone of the remarks made at Edinburgh on the subjact of Imperialis m. There is an impression prevalent both at home and abroad, Lord ROSEBERY says, that the Liberal party is not strenuous in maintaining Imperial responsibility. The existence of that impression cannot be denied. The grounds for it are entirely another matter. It was a legend with no historic foundation. The Liberal party is always prepared to face Imperial responsibility in a spirit of justice, firmness, and anxious care for the future of the Empire. If Lord ROSEBERY is satisfied with that—and what more is there that he can desire? —there can be nothing but a happy issue from that conference of leaders which seems now to be . assured.

It is not possible under any circumstances to condone the use of obscene language, but we have, nevertheless, some sympathy for John Owen, of Runcorn, who was fined for committing this offence on October 27th. Any excuse is said to be better than none, and Owen had an excuse for his profanity which might have moved the Bench to greater leniency than they showed. The allega- tion that one man sat on his stomach for " quite two hours" while another,assisted by the daughters and sons of his wife, removed the furniture from the house, makes it easy to understand that, being only human, he emessed his feelings as strongly as he knew how. And who would not ? Doubtless there are people of so meek a disposition that they would have endured all this without a murmur and metaphorically turned the other cheek to the smiter, but most of us would have followed Owen's example to the extent that our upbringing and sense of decency permitted. A free-born Briton can hardly be expected to endure without complaint the ordeal of having his stomach sat on for "quite two hours," and we think the Runcorn Bench might justly, considering the circumstances of the case, have inflicted a lighter penalty than 10s.

THE ENGLISH CHURCH UNION. Mr. John White and the Education Bill. The annual meeting of the Warrington branch of the English Chutch Union was held in Sr James's schools, Leechford, on Wednesday evening, Mr Joon White, J.P., presiding over a small attendance. The Secretary (Mr C Sawkins Burgess), presented the annual report from which it appeared that the number of members and associates of the branch was 51. The balance sheet submitted by the Treasurer (Mr Bolton) showed an adverse balance of £1 03 Id. The officers were elected as follows :—Cbairman, Mr John White; Viee-chairman,Rev W Stanton ; Secretary, Mr C 8 Burgess; Treasurer.Mr James Bolton; committee. Revs J HG Hffiingsvorth and AS Cameron, Messrs H N Houghton and G Egerton Warburton. The enemies, in the course of his address, extended a welcome on behalf of the branch to the Rev F It Pear- son, the new Vicar of St. James's. He proceeded to refer to the I,iverpool Cathedral scheme, and said the Committee, of wbich he was a member, was working slowly, but he hoped surely. Although they were sur- rounded by difficulties—Me greatest difficulty being to get a proper arobitect—he believed they would eventu- ally be able to erect a very noble building. Speak,ne of the Education Bill, Mr White said there was one point he bad thought it unnecessary to allude to before, • because it was so small that he thought it was dying out, but he saw it was revived again a few nights ago. That was, the state- ment that the bill was the product of or originated with the High Church party. Any statement more foolish than that he could not imag,ine. It was true that the High:Church party and the Lew Church party he might say had accepted the Bill as a moderate solution of a great tdifficulty, with the determination to make the beet of it and so they should make the best of it if it was allowed to pass in anything like its present form and if no more concessions were made. But when they saw concession after concession being made, with no good resultiog from them,—because the agitating meet- ings went on as usuel—and a very important concession was made the other night, a very serious one indeed, be thought instead of the High Church party being the originators of the Bill it might be found out in the future that the English Caurch Union would have to lead a revolt against the Bill. He hoped that was the last ooncession that was going to be made, and that even that might be revoked because it was really a most serious matter as regarded the future of the Voluntary schools and the religious teaching. It might be imagined from the remarks made in the papers and the speeches that were made that the sole object of the Bill was to destroy School Boards and to make religious teaching compulsory in every school in the country. That was exactly contrary to what the Bill was intended to create. Board Schools would be left practically exactly as they were and, religious teaching would be left pre- cisely as it was, so they hoped, in Voluntary schools wsth the Exception of the concession made the other evening. If the Bill did not pass he would ask what position it; opponents were going to be in. Did they prefer to have thinge remain as they were or would they prefer to have a modified Bill which gave them a certain amount of control over the schools? He thought the position of Churcimeople, which they must maintain, was this. These schools had been °rectal by Churchpeop'e. Churchpeople were per- fectly willing that secular education of the best possible description should be carried on in them,but they would reserve and must reserve the right to teach religion in their owls Schools. He thought it Was only fair and reaseeable that when they had provided the schools for secular education free for the country, they should in some way participate in the rates which were paid to Board schools. It would be perfectly unjust if any other course were adopted. Although it was said over and over again that the Bill was for the benefit of Ceurchpeople he ventired to think that the calls upon Churcbpeople When the Bill was passed would be quite as great in future as they had been in the past. If any extension of schools had to be made it would have to be paid for out of the pockets of Chercbpeople. They would have to provide the schools and maintain them and they were saving the country the sum of twenty millions of money. Surely in return for that, it Was only fair that secular education should be paid for in the same way that it was paid for in Board Schooli. Mr W W HILL delivered an address on "Some thoughts on the government of the Church." At the outset he referred to the Education Bill and said Church people had been chargsd with being engaged in the great conspiracy against toe reference to the matter of well-beingEduationof tihheapteoophlaergine was an abomin Age falsehood. There Was no portien of the inhabitants of the couti trywhich had done a more persistent, a more healthy, urto noble work for edUcation than Church y. u people,particularly the clergy. Alluding to Colonel Kenyon-Slar o ,haBu amendmentsaid i thated s uo whole position. the which was faru was carried on Friday, the speakertas Churchpeople were cencernrd, position. The amendment made it possible for the clergymen to be ousted from the Church school as a teacher of religion. It ran clean against the divine com- mission to the clergy to teach,andlit was to be resisteda all cost& No English clergyman could tolerate such an outrage as that. Be thought that before many hours were over the Government would be sorry that they had been so ill-advised. Churcbpeople were face to face with a ,very serious difficulty. Of course they did not wish to close their schools, but they were not going to be robbed of them. They must do everything they could to Strengthen the hands of these in Parliament who would see that the matter was re-considered at the report stage of the Bill and should it be necessary it was also their duty to make a very strong effort to get the Bill so amended in the House of Commons,that it would not present those features of gross injustice,to the trustees and mantigcre of esisting voluntary schools. Dealing with the subject of his address, Mr Hill said the laity had no rights at all in regard to the government of the church, which had been settled by divine authority. It was committed by our Lord to His Apostles and their successors the Bishops to be held by them for all timc. When he said the laity had no rights in regard to the government of the church, they must not think him so foolish as to imagine that .they had no business what- ever to interest themsesves 'n everything that concerned the well being of the church. Laymen had every right to be Consulted in certain matters, and they had every right to use their proper and legitimate influence, but influence was not government. It was, however, Of the highest importance that those upon whom by divine authority was cast the duty of govern- ing the Church, should be accurately informed as to the trend of thought in the minds of the laity. In the course of a long address the speaker advocated the restoration

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL. Mr G Hayes at the above weekly meeting gave an excellent paper on "An Ideal Mutual Improve- ment Class." There was a very lively discussion at the close Messrs W Millington, Cox, Saunders and ' other taking part. ELLESMERE-STREET DEBATING SOCIETY. A interesting lecture on "Art " was given at the above debating class on Friday by Mr J Douglas. There was a very interesting discussion Mr W H Leathwood being the principal speaker. MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. The weekly concert was held at the Seamen's Institute. There was a fair attendance, Mr James Shaw got the party together, the artistes hailing from Birmingham, Liverpool, Frodsham, St Helens, and Widnes. A capital programme was rendered and was very much appreciated by all present. Several members of the Weston Point works band also contributed. Mr Ellis Gatley occupied the chair, and spoke very highly of the mission work. RUNCORN JURYMEN AND THE VIEWING OF BODIES. A number of Runcorn jurymen recently asked Coroner Dobson to alter the arrangement by which they were compelled to assemble at the Police Station before going to view a body. It was urged that if jurymen were allowed to proceed straight to the house where the body lay much time would be saved and inconvenience obviated. Mr. Dobson pro- miEed to consider the matter. The jurymen sum- moned to an inquest on Saturday were allowed to view the body before the Coroner arrived,and when he did put in an appearance the inquest was pro- ceeded with immediately. A MAINTENANCE ORDER. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, George Ellison, jun., of Middlesborough, Yorkshire, was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute to the maintenance of his father and stepmother, who have become chargeable to the common funds of the Union. He did not appear.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr F Johnson) read a letter from defendant, who said he was totally unable to pay anything. He had a wife and five children, and was in debt through being out of work.—Mr J Frodsham, who prosecu- ted on behalf of the Guardians, said defendant wrote in September that he did not intend to pay. During the last nine weeks his wages had been 30s 2d.—An order for is a week and the costs was made.

A. RUNCORN (..tIRL DROWNED IN TRH CANAL. Mr Dobson,district coroner, conducted an inquiry at Runcorn on Saturday into the circumstances attending the death of Amelia Boden, seven years of age, of 22, Taylor's-row, Runcorn, who was drowned in the Bridgewater canal on Thursday evening.—Ann Boden, the mother, said the child went to school on Thursday afternoon. She had not returned home at six o'clock in the evening and witness went to the fair-ground to search for her. She heard nouhing of her and gave information to the police. The child generally came home along the canal bank. She should have gone along Halton-road and witness had told her many a time to do so.—Jennie Clarke, five years of age,said she was at school with the deceased on Thursday. They were going home along the canal bank when witness ran after deceased who fell into the canal. Witness was very frightened and ran away. She told the teacher the next morning— William Byfield said he received information from the police and recovered the body from the canal opposite the Forester's Arms at 10.25 on Friday morning —P.C. Wilding said there were cute and bruises on the face which had evidently been caused by the propellers of passing beats.—A ver- , diet of Found drowned "was returned. Sin J. T. BRUNNER OPENS GOLF LINKS AT WINNINGTON. On Saturday Sir J T Brunner, M.P. opened the new links of the Mid-Cheshire Golf Club, which are splendidly situated at W innington, Northwich. Captain H I Thompson, captain of the Forest Club,• which the Mid-Cheshire Club has replaced, wel- comed Sir John in the name of the Club, and challenged him to a nine-hole game. Sir John said he was delighted with the idea that a golf club had been started at Winnington, and was much pleased with the name they had adopted. He was proud of , having been invited to become the first president, but what he had to do as captain he did not know. He was a strong advocate of golf and enjoyed the game immensely, but unluckily for himself he did not begin until he was close upon his 50th year, and it was hardly possible for a man who began so late to become proficient, though he had heard of a man who began at 54 and got down to scratch. Golf had been described by those who would not play it as a selfish ' game. But golf was often played as a foursome, and in such a game there was absolutely no selfishness. It was a game which a man could carry on almost as long as he could carry on fishing.—(Laughter He had himself been very handsomely beaten by a gentleman of 72, and he knew well of a gentleman of 75 who was the effective captain of no fewer than fourteen clubs.—(Laughter.) Then he got married.—(Laughter.) He remembered with very great interest and pleasure that his first sight of Winningten was when nearly forty years ago he Came to play a game of cricket for Widnes against Northwich. He did his best to beat Northwich,but since then he had done his best to make Northwich beat other places.—(Applause.) He trusted that that change of venue was satisfactory to them as to him.—(Applause.) He was delighted to join the club, he hoped to make very great us of it, and he wished it many years of prosperity. Sir John Brunner then played a nine-hole game with Captain Thompson, the Captain winning an exciting con- test by two holes.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDA V- NOVEMBER 7, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDA V- NOVEMBER 7, 1902
JUBILEE OF THE RUNCORN
tAUTHORII Y.

Fifty years ago on Monday the Runcorn local authority came into being. It was therefore fitting and proper that the jubilee of the authority should be celebrated in the best manner possible. In the afternoon Mr S Taylor, the Chairman of the Council, turned on the water to the water tower on the common, which has been erected to give an ade- quate supply of water to Weston and Weston Point. Subsequently be planted a Coronation oak on the Common opposite the Common cottages, and in the evening the past and present members of the Council met at dinner in the Technical Institute at the invitation of Mr Taylor. •

THE WESTON- WATER TOWER. The new water tower which the Council have had erected for Weston and Weston Point has been built on a point 250 feet above ordnance datum. The tower itself is of stone, and above it is a tank having a capacity of 25,000 gallons. The tank is supplied by means of a special double ram pump from the Runcorn Heath Pumping Station, and the arrangements are of such a character that the men driving the large engines will also attend to the new tower. The supply to Weston is by means of a connection from the tank to the existing main, crossing Heath-road. The cost of the erection, &c., has been about £l,lOO, and the work has been carried out from plans prepared by and under the supervision of Mr Weston, the water engineer. The principal contractors were Messrs T Robinson and Sons and Messrs Tinnions. Formerly the water supply to Weston was intermittent on account ?of the height of the place, but henceforth the whole of the district will have an adequate supply. The .water was turned on to the tank by Mr 8 Taylor, and among others present were the Rev Canon Wood (chairman of the Weston Parish Council), and Messrs J Pritchard, J R Frith, W Handley,R H Posnett, F Lake, E Marshall, J Wilding, J Wilson, F Wiswall, T Jones, E Galley, S Walton, J B Chad- wick, E J Guest, J Tudor, T E C Parkes, .1 J Shaw, M J Sweetman, D Bisbrown, J Collier, and T C Price. Mr J Pritchard explained that it was some few years since the Runcorn authority took over the water works undertahing, and since that time numerous improve- ments had been made, but he might say that large lengths of mains and pipes had been cout,cleaned and re- laid. There had been adopted throughout the district system of valves by which means the water could be I turned off in very limited districts. In the old days when any repairs had to be effected men would go over the whole district and inform the inhabitants that the water would be turned, off probably for twelve or even twenty-four hours. There was nothing of that character now owing to the system of valves, and the public had a supply of water that was almost without limit. In addition to that the town had been divided into six districts, and waste water meters had been laid down, so that leakages might be promptly indicated. Formerly a leakage might perhaps go on for months before it was discovered. By the present arrangement s leakage in any part of the town was immediately ascertained. They would notice also that a reservoir recorder house had been erected, and also that the Runcorn and Halton reservoirs had been cleaned out and necessary repairs done. Since 1896 he found that no less than one and a quarter miles of new mains had been laid. This water tower had been ereoted en- tirely to afford Weston a constant and permanent supply of water. According to an old Act they were only obliged to supply to the height of the present reservoir. The Runcorn people were, however, good enough to have this work undertaken, and it would not cost the inhabitants of Weston anything. The waterworks undertaking was not now owned by a private company, neither was it a commercial undertaking. The construc- tion of this tower would be borne by the Runcorn rate- payers, though he was not quite sure that a Parliamen- tary Committee would consider that they were compelled to bear the whole of the burden Their Weston friends would, therefore, agree that they had very good and generous neighbours in the Runcorn ratepayers. Since the waterworks undertaking came into the hands of the District Council they had expended a total sum of about £4,000 in improvements. They could congratulate themselves upon the abundance of their supply. Neighouring towns had suffered from a scarcity of water at times, but during the driest season they in Runcorn had always had an unlimited supply. There was never any fear of a water famine in this dis- trict. He considered that the waterworks undertaking, was ttip most valuable asset the Council had. In addi- tion td paying for the working expenses and the Con- stant improvements which had been carried out under Mr Wilding's supervision during the last nine years,cost- ing £4,000, they had also had to provide for the interest on the purchase money and sinking fund and yet, he was glad to say that their sinking fund now amounted to £5,000. That money bad actually been sat aside and invested, and during the whole of the period he had named they had had only £734 from the rates. That was at the rate of 4d in the pound covering the period of nine years. He had now pleasure in asking Mr Taylor to turn en the water to the Cover in commemoration of the jubilee of the Runcorn authority. (Applause). Mr Taylor then turned on the water amid applause. He said he was delighted as chairman of the Urban District Council to take part in this proceeding. He had watched the work in connection with the water undertaking since the Council took it over very closely. He had had a good deal to do with it, and it was one of the best speculations. But he did not look at it in that light ; still it was one of the finest undertakings the town could have taken over, and it would be more and more appreciated every year. They knew that in the old days—he was not going to say anything which would reflect against the old company— g-ere were many parts of the town whiah had no water and that large portions of pipes were entirely blocked They had bad to renew them, and as Mr Pritehard had told them, put a mile and quarter of pipes down. They could do without gas in Runcorn if necessary, but water they could not do without. It was a necessity for domestic and sanitary purposes,and so far as the latter was concerned he could say that Runcorn had never been so healthy as during the last few years. Be claimed, therefore, that the water undertaking was most essential, and he felt sure that in the future the Runcorn people would say that the Commissioners did the:right:thing in taking it over. They had now between tour and five thousand pounds, and it was not on paperOaut money they were receiving interest for. They were delighted to have made this provision for Weston. As Mr Pritchard bad said, they were not bound to do it, and many people might not have done it. Their great desire was that Weston, Weston Point and Halton should have the supply they expected to have. They wanted no praise for what they had done, but they hoped that tee people of these dis- tricts would recognize their efforts to give everyone satisfaction. (Applause.) Mr Wiswall proposed, and Mr Wilson seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr Taylor. Canon Wood supported, and the vote was carried with acclamation, Mr Taylor briefly replying. PLANTING THE OAIC.

The company then proceedod to the Common. Mr It El Posnett, on behalf of the town, asked Mr Taylor to plant the oak. He said that Mr Taylor bad for several years been chairman of the committee:which had done all the work in connection with the Common. He perhaps more than anyone, had advocated the making of the Common a pleasure and .a joy to the people of Runcorn, and both he and everyone else would eel that the expen-litu re upon the Common had been juatified. While they were grateful to Mr Taylor and the committee for what they had done, they were also grateful to Mr Wildieg. That gentleman was here sur- rounded by all the wark he had done for the town, and it would remain as a permanent monument of his work. kApplanse.) Mr laylor, having planted the oak in the most work- manlike style, declared the tree planted, he hoped,faith- fully and well. He explained that the ceremony should have taken place on June 26, alluded to the cause of its postponement, and went on to say that they had double occasion for carrying it through that day. They planted the tree in commemoration of the Coronation and of the jubilee of the governing body of Runoorn. He hoped the tree would grow well, and that the people of Runuorn would for many years be able t 3 look upon it with pleasure. (Applause.) Mr Handly proposed and Mr T Jones seconded a vote of thanks to Mr Taylor which was heartily carried. Mr Taylor acknowledged the vote which concluded the ceremony. In the evening there was a fitting climax to the fore- going ceremony. The gathering which tookplace at the Technical Institute was,very appropriately described as a Reunion of the oldlcommissionors and the councillors. The dinner was served in the Art Rem which was very tastefully decorated. Mr S Tayor (chairman of the Council) presided. He was supported on the right by , Alderman S il Hazlehurst, Mayor of Birkenhead (a past ' member) and on the left by Mr R H Poenett (vice-chair- man) of the Coated. There were alsi preknt Messrs E Imison, W Handley, M J Sweetman, G H Kirkham, E Galley, T Jones, J Wilson, F Wiswall, J H Saltteld,lB Walton, E Bisbrown,J J Shaw, and Cr Hewitt (present members), J HorsefiAd. W Hankinson, H J Grief) J J Speakman, T Lea, J Meadowcrof 0, W Fustier and T Morris (past members), F A Lake,. law clerk ; E Mar- shall, secretary ; J Wilding surveyor ; M Barker, con- sulting surveyor ; W Jones, c3ief clerk ; and J Carter, treasurer (officials) ; and F J Norman, J R Frith, J M Frith, and J Lawrenson (headmaster of the Technical Schools.) After a Well served dinner which was catered for by Mr J Lea. Letters of regret for enforced absence were read from Mr John Simpson, Glen Morpha,Conway,Dr McDougall, Messrs T Harris, Bowdon, E Wynne Humphreys, Lon- don and Dr Gastaldi' Lydbury North. A number of toasts were afterwards honoured to the accompaniment of the usual speech making. Mr W Handley proposed The post—the Runcora

Improvement Commissioners." Mr Handley enumer- ated the industries of Runcorn 50 years ago, and said Runcorn bad progressed greatly since that time, and if the present Councillors or successors of the Commis- sioners were true to their trust and emulated the work and virtues of their predecessors, then they would make the linked past The stepping stones on which to rise To higher, nobler things.

(Applause.) Alderman Hazleleurst, in a felicitous and humorous speech, responded. Messrs Frith and Meadoccroft also responded. Mr Fisher proposed " The present—the Council and its Chairman." He said he was a Commissioner for thirteen years and was very sorry when the time came for him to separate himself from it. He had followed with great interest the proceedings of the present Council and he felt sure that the old Board bad every reason to be proud of its successors. (Applause.) Mr Shaw, the youngest member of the Council, responded. Mr Taylor, who was received with applause, also responded. He said that since the old Board the work of the Council had increased almost tenfold. They had taken over the Burial Board management, the appoint- ment of overseers, and a technical day school, which was a matter of the first importance. They had been made, also, a portion of the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority, which meaat additional responsibility. The Council was undoubtedly doing good work. And he was delighted to hear so much said about the Old Board of which he was one out of six members present. Their duty aas to ensure the health of the people and to keep down the rates. (Applause.) Mr Wiswall proposed" The future—may it increase and prosper." Messrs Raison, Pritchard, Bisbro wn, and Wilson responded. Mr Posuett proposed "The Officials," arid paid a high compliment to them for their valuable services. Mr Taylor, on behalf of the Council, presented to Mr Marshall copies of Chamber's Encyclopedia and Scot's works ; to Mr Wilding, Chamber's Encyclopedia and the "Cathedrals of England," and to Mr Walter Jones a revolving bookcase. fir, eulogized their work and Spoke in appreciativee terms of them personally. Messrs Marshall, Wilding, and Jones responded. The proceedings concluded with the singing of the National Anthem, and three cheers for the chairman.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A COURESPONDENT.]

The jubilee dinner of the Urban Council given on Monday night by Mr. S. Taylor (Chairman of the Authority) was unquestionably one of the most brilliant functions that has ever been held in Run- corn. In every sense it was worthy of the occa- sion,of the Council and of Mr Taylor, the host. The majority of the speeches were of a high order. Some merged into the brilliant Mr Handley's his- toric knowledge of the town served him in excel- lent stead, and his was one of the most interesting contributions to tho evening's entertainmsnt. The speech of the evening was unquestionably Alder- man liazelburst's. From the first line to the last it was thoroughly literary, enlivened by a rare touch of humour. Needless to say Mr. Taylor was in rare form, and contributed by his practical remarks and witty sallies in no small degree to the interest of the function. The jubilee day was a great day for the city fathers, and they rose to the occasion right manfully.

It is especially pleasing to notice the happy bond of sympathy between the officials and the Council. Few men are more esteemed in Runcorn than Messrs E Marshall, J Wilding, and W Jones. The greater Council of Runcorn citizens will be rejoiced to think that these are the men whom the Council have delighted to honour—by presenting them with serviceable mementos of their work. May they live long to enjoy their honours!

I wish to call the attention of the public to a letter published in another column from Mr FJ Norman. The letter' apparently, has been called forth by the speech of Mr Hazlehurst who at the opening of the church bazaar laid all the blame for the sectarian strife in Runcorn on the shoulders of those who , would not follow the lead of the broad-minded Hugh Price Hughes. I think it must conceded that Mr Norman satisfactorily disposes of that idea and traces the root cause of all the petty jealousy at the present moment to Canon Wood who, in the years that are fled, refused to meet the Rev Hugh Price Hughes in Runcorn, on a mission work which could not, in the least, be said to have a sectarian purpose. It is the intolerant cleric and not the Non- conformist who is responsible for a divided Run- corn, which at one time used to be rather a happy place.

Coroner Dobson has made an important con- cession. He actually allowed jurymen the other day to view the body before the formal opening of the inquiry. Let us be thankful that at times officials do manage to escape from the thraldom of red tape.

Apropos of the Church bazaar. I have been told that raffling—in other words gambling—was carried on to a very large extent, the stakes, in some in- stances, being as low as one penny and one half- penny. Some couple of years ago I believe the police stopped, one Christmas-tide, all the trades- folk from raffling their perishables on the ground that is was illegal. Being a layman in these matters I naturally ask why, if these two instances be true, should the tradesfolk be prohibited from gambling when the church, a spiritual organization, is per- mitted to gamble in precisely the same method? There is something rotten in the state of Denmark when an abuse is tolerated in high quarters and disapproved in the humbler folk I

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

It was a sore disappointment to the Linnetts to be beaten at Salford on Saturday by a much in- ferior team. The game was not of a very high order and Runcorn were easily the superior. Hun- dreds had Oleft the field thinking that Runcorn were the winners when the home team scored on the close of time. It is hard lines but as Jacob Faithful wmild say " Better luck next time."

There is sure to be a tough struggle at Irwell- lone on Saturday, when Halifax who has not yet had their lines crossed meet the Linnetts. Runcorn is playing a fairly representative team and with luck should pull off the match,

div.head: WATER. -- The Earlestown Supply.
div.p: WATER. -- The Earlestown Supply.
Local Government Board Inquiry.

Last Friday Mr A AG Malet, M. Insr.C. E., conducted a Local Government Board inquiry at the Town Hall, Earlestown into the application of the Earlestown and Newton Urban District Council for sanction to borrow £1,779 paid out of revenue from the 14 April, 1897, to the 30th Bepternner, 1901. There were present :—Messrs W Collingwood (chairman of the Council), T Ormand (vice-chairman), C B F Barron (chairman of the Water Committee), Doctors Latham and Patterson, Councilhra E T Evans and Thompsob, Messrs Read and Waring (consulting engineers to the Council), C Cole (clerk), A Bowes (surveyor), W T Surtees (water engineer), J Rigby, sen., J Rigby , jua, and a number of inhabitants from Park Side.

div.head: CLERK'S REPORT.
div.p: THE CLERK'S REPORT.

_ The report of the Clerk showed that the rateable value of the district is £69.481, and the assessable value £57,754. The population aceording to the 1901 census was 16,699, and at the present time it is estimated at 17,250. The area of the district is 3,103 acres. The amount of out-standing loans are as follows :—General Department, £9,982 Ils lid ;Ges Department, £9,919 Os 7d ; Water Department, £6,807 3s 4d ; total, £26,708 155 101. The rates in the district are :—General Improvement Rate, is 3d in the £ ; Highway Rate, 7d in the £ ; Water Rate,3i in the. ; total,rate 29 Id.—As this inquiry is supplementary to the ine airy held by Colonel Coke on the 6th November last wain reference to the application which had been made to the Local Government Board, for their sanction to the borrowing of £23,150, to defray the cost of carrying out certain works in order to complete the Councils echeme,for the provision of a proper supply of water to the inhabitants of the distriet, and at which inquiry no objection was made by any person to the scheme then submitted. These estimates were prepared by the late engineer to the Council. The Council then went more fully into the question of the appointment of Engineers to superintend the carrying out of the proposed works and engaged Messrs Read and Waring of West minater as their engineers for this work, which step was taken with the view of obtaining the best possibm advice on their undertaking. As this appointment was made shortly before the last inquiry the engineers had not then gone fully into the scheme. It was pointed out to Colonel Coke that owing to the breakdown which had taken place and which had arisen from mechanical defects in the pumping machinery—since remedied—the supply had not been continuous, that the Council had on several occasions been compelled through the want of duplicate machinery to obtain water from the London and North Western Railway Company, and that they were most anxious to proceed with the completioe of their scheme as quickly as possi le. Since the holding of the Inquiry above referred te,the engineers have gone more fully into the subject and have modified the scheme to a considerable extent both in regard to economy and efficiency. By the old scheme it was proposed to con- struct a service reservoir to hold 500,000 gallons, in a field near to the Common and a high service tank, ta hold 50,000 gallons alongside the service reservoir, also a pumping main from the existing pumping station to the proposed service reservoir with a branch to the high service tank. It was afterwards found that the level of the ground in the field suggested, was not sufficiently high for this purpose and that as a high service reser- voir was required it could be more economically erected at the pumping station and thus save the purchase of additional land for this purpose. The high service task could then be dispensed with. As regards the diminu- tion in the capacity of the proposed reservoir, the engineers considered that one of 300,000 gallons or one days supply would be adequate to meet all requirements and give a reasonable margin for future increase in the demands of the district. As the present engines and pumps in the two boreholes are capable of pumping this amount of water they will only in the future be required to pump for 12 hours daily and thus the new and the ' old machinery being equal in capacity, they could be n °riled alternate days, either set being sufficient to raise the required quantity of water. The supply would be by gravitation. The material of the structure of the proposed reservoir has also been altered from brick to ferro concrete, the cost of which will be a considerable saving. With respect to this materiel, the engineers reported that 2hey bad no hesitation in recommending its adoption and from personal inspections made by them both at home and abroad, of several reservaire constructed of that material, they were satisfied as to its suitability. The alteration of the site of the proposed reservoir has consequently needed a re-arrangement of distribution mains. The cost of the amended scheme as compared with the old scheme is as follows : Am'ded se'me. Old sc'me £. 2,700 ... 2,700
New well and headings ... Pumps and engines and extension of engine house ... High service reservoir ... Elevated tank Pumping main Distributing mains ... Two cottages

As no objection was raised by the Local Government Board to the plans of the new well it was desirable that the work should be proeeeded with befere the other works were commenced, the council entered into a con- tract for the work and it has so far progressed that the sinking has been completed to a deeth of 190 feet from which depth the headings are now being driven. The Local Government Board, in view of the urgency of the pipe laying being commenced at once have sanctioned a sum of £2,000 being borrowed on account of this work, but the work cannot be proceeded with until the site of the proposed reservoir has been approved by the Board. The present works consist of two bore- holes with horizontal engine actuating a pump in each borehole, discharging into a covered tank of 200,000 gallons capacity, and a s.parate quadruple acting force pump to deliver a maximum quantity of 24,000 gallons per hour into the district. The water has been analysed by Dr Campbell Brown, the Liverpool Analyst, and declared to be good. A bacteriological examination has been made by Professor Delepine of Owens College, Manchester, who has pro- nounced the water to be absolutely safe for drinking purposes. The Council obtained tho advice of Professcr Boyd Dawkins D.Sc F.R.S. before proceeding with the sinking of the well, as to the supply of water likely to be obtained at the site. The Professor stated that the priaesic sandstones of the district are highly charged with water and that, in his opinion, an ample supply for the needs of the district may be obtained within the area of the present site. He also approved of the Coun- cil's proposal to sink a well to be connected with the borings by edits by which means,the present yield would be most probably more than doubled—that is to niece than 500,000 gallons per day. So far this opinion appears to be confirmed. The yield now for the two boreholes andthe well (without adits) is over 300,000 gallons per day of 24 hours, When the edits have been driven to col- lec' the water, this amount,it is anticipated,will be over 500,000 gallons. Taking the present estimated popula- tion at 17,253, this quantity works out to 29 gallons per head. Of the: 300,000 gallons now raDed, 221,000 gallons only are distributed ; the I)ss is accounted for by the working operations rendering some of the water unfit for domestic use, the district at the present time being supplied with 13 gallons per head of population. It is considered, owing to the fact that there are very few w.c's and baths in this district, that 300,000 gallons of water will be ample to supply the daily needs of the inhabitants—this quantity working out to 17 gallons per head per day. The amount of money the Council may borrow under their Local Act as amended by the Local Government Boards Provisional Orders Confirmation (No. 2) Act of 1901, for the purposes of the water undertaking,and on the security of the revenue of the water undertaking and of the District Fund and General District rate, or upon either of such securities is £25,000, The Clerk said that both bores would !give a good supply. The period for which they asked the advance was 30 years from the date of the sanction. The Inspector : I will put that before the Board.

think it probable that they will give a shorter period than that under the circumstances of the case. The Clerk : They granted a similar application with respect to the Gas Department. The period for repay- ment was 16 years. Mr Cole also stated that the total money expended up to date was £960, on the sinking of the well and edits. The Inspector asked what was the population for the last two or three decades. The Clerk ; In 1871, pOOO ; 1881, 10,580 ; 1891, 12,861 ; 1901, 16,699. The estimated population fcr 1902 is 17,250. The Inspector asked if there were any houses in the , district situate.] too high to be Fervee.

The Clerk : No, sir: The Inspector : There will be a constant 4eroice everywhere ? The Clerk : It is anticipated that that will be so. The Inspector : What will be the greatest pressure in the distributing mains ? Mr Rsad : The greatest pressure we have is 115 ft. The Inspector : What will that be in pounds to the square inch ? Mr Read : About 50. The Inspectm : What is your specification ? Mr Read : The pipes are tested to 250 feet, Cr 107 lb. per square inch. The plans of the borehole, /cc., were then produced and explained by Mr Read. Mr Read stated, in answer to the Inspector, that the engines would be able to pump 25,000 gallons per hour into the service reservoir. They only intended to work one set of engines at a time, but they could get suffi- cient steam pressure to work both. The old engines would only pump 12,500 gainers per hour. Ths old , engines were three years old, and toad been working a little over two years. Mr Cellingwood : The borehole pumps were put down as the cheapest wave of seeertaining whether water was there. We found the water was there, and we are
going in for this improved sod economical scheme and more efficient and economical pumping airungeme3ts, the expenditure for which has been justified in that we found the water there.

--Mr Read said they were going to make the engine house large enough to put in a second pair of pu:nps and a second duplicate engine. They were merely going to enl age the house so that it would not req aire extend- ing later or. Mr J Bridge, jun., intimated to the Inspector that they were entirely without a water supply at Park Side and they were compelled to cart water some distance for domestic purposes,and also for the cattle. He com- plained that the Council had done nothing to bring about aisatisfactory supply. They had promised since 1900 to put down a water supply. The Inspector said he could not entertain any question relating to past history, and be considered that the Council were doing their best to meet the difficulty. Mr Bridge said it would be all right if the Couneil would carry out the scheme. The Inspector remarked that the scheme of the Coun- cil was very efficient,more so than the previous scheme. It might be hard to the individual, yet the Council had to consider the advantage of many. Dr Latham said he didn't see the use of wasting the time of the inquiry with matters that did not come in the inquiry. The Inspector agreed and remarked that if Mr Bridge wrote to the Local Government Board he would pro- baby get an answer that the Council were doing their best to meet the requirements of the neighbourhood. Mr Borron proposed a vote of thanks to the Inspector for having gone so thoroughly into such details of the scheme, and asked the Inspector to push the matter forward as quickly as possible. Mr Golfing %rood seconded, and said that the Inspector had assisted them considerably by his inquiry in point- ing out what might possibly lead to several improve- ments.
The vote was passed. The Inspector briefly returned thanks.

div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL

Town Ball, Eirlestown on Mondry evening. W Collingwood presided and there wrr3 also present ?dessrs C B F Borron, N Siddeley, W Gilinour, J Simpson, W Thompson, Drs Latham and Patt2rson with C Cole (clerk) Bowes (surveyor) and Surrees (water engineer).

Resolved also that the Chairmen 9f the Finance, Gas, and Water Committees be requested to consider and report as to the financial po ;Rion of the gas and water underta kings. I The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Coun- cillor W Thompson.
WATER C )311AUTTEE.

A letter was read from Mr F W Webb, engineer to the London and Nortb-Western Railway Company, Crewe, stating that the directors had decided that if it was absolutely necessary they woul 1 endeavour to let the Council have a small quantity of water, the price to ,be the same as befov, viz., 18 per 1,000 gallons, but they could not undertake to let them have a full supply or accept any responsibility in the matter. The Clerk reported that Mr J J Poole (contractor) had accepted the Committee's offer for the lowering of the borehole pumps, also that the Contractor had stated that ho would take every precaution for keeping the water in the additional well ebsolutely pure during sink- ing operations. A letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the Council's application tor eanction to borrow £18,900 for the purpose of the water under- taking, and stating that in view of the urgency of the matter they Mad decided to sanction the borrowing of the sum of £2.000 on account, for the purpose of laying distribution mains, which formal sanction (dated the 27th September, 1902) they enclosed. ; The Engineers reported to the committee that they had inspected the work in progress at the Pumping station and that they were satisfied with what had been done. They also stated that it was not advisable to proceed with any part of the main laying until the Local Government Board had approved of the entire scheme, as this question solely depended upon the site of the new reservoir, but if the Committee decided to proceed with the work the nine-inch main to Earlestow n might be laid. It was also resolved that the engineer be empowered to obtain from the London and North-Western Rail way Company sach supplies of water as can he spared by them from time to time to enable a constant supply to be made to the inhabitants during the day. Resolved also that the tender of Messrs Richard Evans and Ce., Limited, for the supply of slack to the Water Works for the period ending the 31st May, 1903, be accepted. HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE.

The surveyor submitted to the committee plan which he had prepared showing the suggested improvements to the corners of the following streets leading out of Earl-street, viz :—(e) the road leading over the Railway Bridge to Vitriol-square. and (b) Alma-street. Resolved : , That the plan be approved, and that the Surveyor be I directed to make arrangements for the carrying out of the work—the corners of the streets to be rounded off as much as possible. ",The Superintendent of the Brigade (Mr R T Suttees) submitted to the committee his report with respect to the organization and working of the Brigade, and also as to tbe proposed charges in connection with the attendance of the Brigade at fires and drills. He also reported tbat he had seen Messrs Reddaway's hose pipes tested to a pressure of 450 lbs.. and that he had given them the order for the supply of twelve 60 feet lengths. Resolved : That the ordering of these hose pipes be approved and adopted. A letter was read from the Local Government Board

with respect to expenditure on the Horse Ambulance, and stated that while the Biard would be prepared to • confer on the Council the general power of accepting gifts on behalf of the inhabitants of the district, they win not aware of any statutory provision which would empower the Council to expend funds raised by means of the General District rate in the maintenance or repair of the Horse Ambulance. A letter signed by certain ratepayers resident in Town Hall VVard,calling the Com- mittee's attention to the bad condition of true footpath 'leading from Viaduct-street to Market-street, was sub- mitted to the Committee.—Resolved—That the Clerk be directed to reply that the footpath will be put in order. The Chairman reported upon the interview which he and the Clerk and Surveyor, together with Mr T Sutton, valuer, had had with Mr C H Marsh and his slicitcr ond valuer, with respect to Mr Marsh's claim for damage done to his land and crops through the laying of a sewer, and that eventually the claim had been settled by Mr Marsh agreeing to accept the final offer of £62 108 in fdll discharge of his claim (£lO2 103) and costs. Slaughter-house licenses were granted to (a) Mr Richard Jones, of 6, Bridge-street, Earlestown, for the use and occupation of premises situate at the Hand and Banner-yard, High-street, Newton-le-Willows ; (b) Mr George Wilde, of 52, Legh-street, Earlestown, for ' premises situate at the back of 52, Legh-street, Earles town, and ; and (c) The Earlestown Industrial Co-oper- ative Society, for their premises in . Suez-street. It appearing that each of the ten houses situate off Vista- road, and known as Hazel Grove, was without a drain sufficient for the effectual drainage thereof, it was resolved that Mr Henry Ashcroft, Inspector of Nuisances be directed to serve notices under Section 23 of the Public Health Act, 1875, upon the owner of the houses to make, within 14 days, a covered drain or drains emptying into the Council's sewer in Vista-road, and that if such notices be not complied with in any case Ithat the work be done by the Council and the expenses incurred by them in so doing be recovered from the owner in a summary manner. GIFTS OF PROPERTY. The Chairman moved the following resolution : That application be made to the Local Government Board for an Order under section 33 of the Local Government Act, 1894, conferring on this Council the powers of a Parish Council under section 8 (1) (b) of the Act, by which the Council will be empowered to accept and ho!d any gifts of property, real or personal, for the benefit of the inhabitants of this drs.trict." Mr Thompson seconded, and it was carried,

He thought it necessary to bring it before the Council or committee so that it might be decided. Mr Si non moved that the application be referred the General Purposes Committee. Mr Gilmour seconded: Carried. This was all the principal business.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

A RESERVIST'S ATTEMPTED SUICIDE' At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday. before Dr Fox (presiding) and Alderman Hutchinson, Arthur Gallop, 29. Powys-street. was &lamed with attempting to commit suicide by cutting his throat with a razor on October 27 Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner who was a married man belonged to the army reserve He had been out to South Africa and returned about two years ago. Since he came back he had been drinking heavily and had not attended to his work as he ought to have done. On the night in question he came borne between seven and eight o'clock under the influence of drink. His mother and his wife were in the house and the mother !poke to him about taking so much drink and not attending to his work. He picked up a poker to strike his mother but his wife prevented him, and both the wife and the mother left the house. They returned in a few minutes, and on looking through the kitchen win- dow SAW the prisoner cutting his throat with a razor. They rushed into the house and together with some neighbours bandaged the wound PC Woods was sent for and took the prisoner to the Infirmary where he remained until the previous day. He now said be was very sorry for what he had done, and he (the superintendent) did not propose to offer any evidence against him.—Prisoner's wife promised to --take care of hlm and he was discharged SMART SENTENCE ON A BRUTAL FATHER. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Thomas Jefferies and Annie Jeffcries, Martin scroft were charged with neglecting their sin children—Mr Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C, and said that on October 22nd Mr Aukland. relieving and school attendance officer, bad occasion to visit defeneant's house with regard to the children's attendance at school. Ifs found a boy and a little baby alone in the house The baby was filthy dirty and lice were crawling over its body. The house was in a filthy state. Mr Aukland reported the matter to Inspector Hackett and he and the Inspector visited, the house on Saturday. The children were alone in the house. The male defendant went out hawking green-grocery. He left the house about nine in the morning and did not return until late at night. The woman said that the first week he went out he never came home sober and spent all the money he earned. She was therefore compelled to go out with him to prevent him spending the money. The wife saw the terrible condition of the children was caused by her having to neglect them in the day time while she went out with her husband. Mr Frank Berfoot, the nuisance inspector for the district, had visited the house. He saw the baby lyinz on a filthy, rotten bed. It appeared that the male defendant had, when under the influence of drink, picked up two of the boys, held them over his head, and thrown them to the floor. The children Ewald they could not live with the man and they hoped he would not come back to the house. On one occasion he committed an assault on his nine year old daughter Evidence in support of this statement was given, Mr Kerfoot stating that the baby was be'na simply poisoned by the smell from the bedding.— Inspector Hackett said the only food In the house ,7SS a ernal! piece of bread and about half an sense of butter. The children were, however, fairly well fed, the neighbours having given them foed.—Mrs Jeffries was called and said she had not time to look after the children, as she bad to go out with her husband from morningtill night. Her husband had on several occasions threatened to murder her —The man denied having ill-treated the children —The Bench com- mitted him to gaol for six months hard labour, the charge against the woman being withdrawn.

POACHING AFFRAY AJ Bitwant—GAMERFHPFRa ATTACKED. An unusual case of poaching was heard at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday Peter Rowson. Bowes-street, was summoned or entering a plantation at Burtonwoed, the property of Lord ',llford. at 4.31 on Sunday morning October 19th, for the purpose of taking game, he being armed with a gnia.—Mr B A White, prosecntel, and said be thought the facts of the case would diselose one of the worst forms of offence that could be committed under Cie game laws and one which was attended by circumstances as aggravated as it was possible for them to be. At half-past four on the Sunday morning in question two gamekeepers in the employ of Lord Lilford were on duty near Bewsey Park, when they heard shots. They separated and ran round the plantation, ttlsich was a roosting and bseeding place tor pheasants and saw the defendant and three other men standing Inside the plantation. Three ef the men were armed with guns, including the defendant. The men ran away when they saw the keeper Lee and then they met Jackson the other keeper who had gone round the other way. The men then raised their guns and threatened to shoot Jackson. Lee came up, and they also threatened to shoot him. Shortly afterwards the men commenced to throw stones at the keepers, to,th of whom were struck, one on the hand and the other on the leg, and then they ran away The keepers followed, and when they got to Child's cottage, Mood-lane, they tried to apprehend the poachers. The men faced round and clubbed their guns, and Rowson struck at the keeper, Jackenn The latter dodged the blow. and the gun fen en the ground. Jackson took possession of it. The men again an away, but the keepers still very pluckily kept to them. and Lee recognized ltowson. He called out to him. Hello, is that you Peter Rowson ?" to which the defendant replied. "Yes, it is me George. I will consider It a favour if you will let me off this time and I will never trouble you again." When they recognized one of the men the keepers did not pursue them further, and en going back to the plan- tation they found a canvas bag, containing a dead pheasant. The d-fendant called at the house of Lee, the keeper, and offered him money to settle the matter. Rowson refused to give the names of the other men. On the follow- ing Monday the defendant's father offered Lee 20s Mr White pointed out the seriousness of the ease and said he thought that 'after hearing the evidence the magistrates would come to the conclusion that the full penalty of three months' imprisonment and an order to find sureties for six months, was none too severe for that case Evidence was given by the gamekeepers, bearing out this statement.—Questioned by Mr Steel, who appeared for the defendaat both witnesses admitted that Rowson's gun was net loaded, but he had had plenty of time to unload it after he was dissevered.—For the defence, Mr Steel said the witnesses for the proeeontion admitted that Idowson's gun was not loaded, and therefore he could not have fired any of the shots. Neither of them saw him throw stones,and he asked the magistrates not to be prejudiced by the general evidenee,—Prisoner was committed to gaol for a month, and ordered to find two sureties of ZIO each for his good behaviour, or, in default, a further three months' imprisonment.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY NOVEMBER 7 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY NOVEMBER 7 1902
PARISH CHURCH SALE OF WORK.
The Rector and the Education Bill.

On Friday afternoon a sale of work in aid of the Parish Church Restoration Fond end Day Schools was opened in Fairfield Schools and will be contidued to- day. There was a large attendaue at the opening ceremony which was performed by Mrs Lyon, of Appleton Hall, in the absence through indisposition of Lady Brooke, of Norton Priory.

div.head: RECTOR AND TEE EDUCATION BILL.
div.p: THE RECTOR AND TEE EDUCATION BILL.

The Rama presided and in the course of his speech announced that Lady Greene% who had originally been asked to open the sale, could not be present, but for- warded a cheque for fifteen guineas. Unfortunately Lady Brooke was prevented from being present through indisposition and they were grateful to Mrs Lynn for opening the sale. Referring hs the object of the sale he said they had raised £2,000 for the improvement of the Parish Church but they needed at least £5OO more, With regard to the day schools, he wanted them to understand that owiner to the requirements of the Board of Education and the municipal authorities they had been involved in a large debt on the scheols throng!" no fault of their own. They were trying to raise that large sum of £1,500 by a voluntary rate and The manufacturers were most kindly and generously coming forward to help them. They eonld not, however, expect to raise the whole amount in that way, and they were trying to supplement the sum already received by that sale, the proceeds of which would be divided between the schools and the Church. They knew that the nreeent was a time of the utmost importance. The Education Bill which had been brought for ward by the Government was in the minds of everyone. They earnestly hoped that the Bill would be passed, not because they thought it would give them anything like that which they ouch` to have, but they thought it was the best BM they could get. He always made a point ef listening te what the other side Is id, and he went to the public meeting in the Parr Hall the other evening. He heard an uneducated man—he called him uneducated because the speaker said be was uneducated —who spoke with great eloquence and could move the /names, and he and others present spoke as he (the Rector) thought rneet unfairly. They said their (Church) schools could not compare in any way with the Board schools. They (churchpeoples) were quite satisfied to stand by the reports of the Government inspector and let him be the judge of whrther their schools were good lor not. The speakers also said that in many schools the managers were only anxious to get a Churchmen, a Catholic, as they called him, on purpose to teach the doctrines, and that the managers did not care in the least about the secular education. He (the Rector) said that was utterly false. There might be some unwise men who pressed unduly certain teaching, and there might be some men who took no interest in their scheels and never went into them, but the majority, he thought, were just as anxious that the very best secular education should be given as well as religious education. Of &huge they wanted sound, thorough Churchmen because they krow the teaching of the church was simply the teaching of the Bible—they knew that for a fact—but they were also most anxious to get intelligent, intellec- tual, cultured teachers in order that they might give the very best secular instruction as well as the very best religious instruction. He had been most anxious to have an opportunity of saving that. He could not tell them how deeply be felt. They knew that he had earnestly and honestly worked the Parish Church schaels that they might have the bast imbnels poasible. They had got most excellent schools—they could not, he thought have better—and it ought to he a very great encourage- ment for everyone to try and do all they could for the success of the sale. In conclusion the Rector cordially thanked all who had assisted in preparing for the sale. Mrs LYON then opened the sale and expressed the hope that it would, like all .Warrington loaners, be success. _

A hearty vote of thanks aZas accorded to Mrs Lyon on the proposition of Mr J 01 Craik seconded by Mr J De.hurat, and the bosiness of the sale was proceeded with. The Ttall9 had besn very tastefully arranged and were laden with a variety of WSTO9. The stallholders were :—Pirozhial stall, Mesdames Willis,Peter Rylands, Willenckg. J Craik, Dewhurst, W Price, Taylor, W Fairclough, Farrell, Holbrook, Range, Evans, R Fair- clongh. and Hall, and Album Boyle, F Price, Brown, Nield. Shaw and Taylor ; St George's Mission, Airs Barrett, Misses Hetherington, M Woods, and A Woods, and the Day and Sunday Ronne! teachers ; St Clement's Mission, Mrs Cameron, Mrs Saunders, Miss Taylor, Miss Audrey Taylor and other.; Children's toy eall. Mr 4 Lowe, Misses F Lowe, V Collin, L Bottom- IPV. G Atherton, M Lows, and Evans. Master T M Price, H Box and G Harding ; all, wig White, Miss E Mrs R Collin and Mrs Rottornler ; china stall, Mrs D Buckton,Mrs Melville, Miss GlSdsSone (Liverpool) and Mien Pierpoint ; flower stall, Mrs John Davies and daughters; lea erelrts et%ll, Misses Howard, Credit, Auklanrl, Lloyd and Whittle ; refreshment stall, Miss Litton, Miss Willis and friends ; fortune telling table, Miss G Hudson ; shooting galleryi Mrs Moreton. During the darentertainments were given and were taken port in by :—Miss Lyon, Mies Edith Gladstone, MIRS Lilian Gladstone Miss Trude Crogfield, Mies Madge Davies, Mr G H Mosley, Mr 11113rintelow, and others. The MaPpOle dame was cleverly performed by the junior classes of the girls' higher grade school.

div.head: Rector Again Refers to the Education Question.
div.p: The Rector Again Refers to the Education Question.

The sale of work ic aid of the Wsrrington Parish Church Restoration Fund and Day Schools was re- opened in Fairfield Schools on Saturday afternoon by Mrs Frost, of GraPPPlab,ll• The RECTOR airain explained the objects of the sale and said that £5OO at least were required for each of them. Speaking of the schools be said he wanted his hearers to think over what had been said at liffereitt meetings lately with reference to education. He csuld not tell thorn how it had stirrsi hint. Re heard an ignorant bur very eleq lent msn su•altirig about priest- craft the other day and Raying that the real object of churcheerible woe to try and make us* of their day schools as means of making converts to the Chureh. That wog utterly untrue. They were most intennely anxious to have the very best secular educa- tion that they could p,siibly give, and, as he said on Friday. they were quite contsnt to abide by the report of the Government Inspecto% They were not biassed men ; they were not prejudiced in favour of church- peaces. The inspectors gave them just what they deserved according te the results. He believed they had as oxeallent day schools is it was tootaible to find— quits as glod oe any Baird Sehoole. Me had received that day the report on their poorest schools, where the children naid ne feet. They had earned the highest grant of 17s per head upon an average of 245 ehildren. which made a total grant of £21.4 51. Wag net that a geed answer re be able to sine ? It was such absurd nonsense to sneak about nrietrartft Dii they think the parents of the 2.000 children in their Sunday echos!s wield send those children when there Will as possible compulsion if they did nit believe in th•ir olergy and Sunday school ? God worked in grace as in nature through moans. In the spiritual world God had appointed the sacramental system, church and the ministers, as means of grace, inesns of supplying biassing to His people. They (his hearers) knew what religious instruction must be where they had En cut out almost evervthingto please everybody. They (ehurchpeople) were net going to do anything of the kind. They were going to teach the truth, the whole truth and nething but the truth in their ',chords. They were intensely anxious that their schools should supply net only the very best religious inetractien but the very best secular instruction too. In opening the sale Mrs Frost expressed the hope that all present would do their best for Its success.

W E ATKIN proposed/a vote of thanks to Mrs Frost, Speaking as treasurer of the schools, he said he hoped those prereht weuld realise how very inuca the yoluns tarp sehnols wprs in need of their support still. The Eincation fill mioht do a groat sisal for voluntary schools but he thought he was quite right in saying that it was not at all a Biil which the clergy would have wished to have passed. They did not rush at it and moan it up greedily at all. They accepted it as the best Bill that eould be brought! forward. .
_ Mr TAYL,R sPc)nded and the motion was heartily, carried, Mrs Frost briefly responding.
Two bows to the course of construction at First' near Brumele, collapsed on Tuesday,burying eight work- men. Five bodies have been recovered, and it is feared the remaining three aro dead.

div.head: REV J YONGE'S 26TH ANNIVERSAIY.
div.p: THE REV J YONGE'S 26TH ANNIVERSAIY.

Sunday last witnessed the 26th anniversary of the Rev John Yonge's pastorate at Wycliffe Congregational Churb. Referenee was made to this interesting occa- sion by the pastor at the morninv. service. He based his discourse on the text " Thy loving kindnese is Defers mine eyes " (Psalm 26, Dart of verse 3). There was a peculiar interest,he geld, attaching to the first Sunday in Nevember both for huntelf and the cnngreg ation,in the feet that it was then' 28th anniversary of their mutual relationship, and also the 40'AI anniversary of his ministerial life. When he began work there in 1876 the morning conv.roaatioa we m Joh lor !or than it had become now. The habit of sanctuary attendance was mere marked than it was now. Since that day owner- one had been the changes in their midst. Of the six deacons then in office two had bean removed from them, three had passed away, and one only remained. Of the church nsembership, which then numbered nearly 180 persons only 35 were included in their present member- ship of nearly 400,end amongst meat-holders and scholars there had been a very similar aggregate of change. Looking bank still further to the des' when he began his ministerial career in November 1862, of the men who left college on the same day wits himself, he (Mr. Yong.) was the only one left in the world. Tee preacher proceeded to point out that the futur was not ours but God's, and helpful assurance came from the retrospect which told them of the loving-kindness of the Lord. Hops even,' immortal in the Christian breast, end it wee a hope that would never make eehamed.—ln the evening, the subject of Mr. Yonge's diseourse was " Invitation—the attitude of the gospel and the supremo work of the Church." The text with which he introduced the subject was chosen from Revelation 22ad ehapt.r, part of the 17 v. " Let him that heareth say come." The preacher pointed out that he desired on that anniversary to strike once mere the kay-nete of personal service in the cause of Jesus Christ. He pleaded for mere aggressive work by the members of the Church and congregation in reaching those outside the churches.

div.head: UNDERGROUND TELEGRAPH CABLE. Laying of the Mains to Warrington Completed.
div.p: THE UNDERGROUND TELEGRAPH CABLE. Laying of the Mains to Warrington Completed.

The Post-office is new in a position to announce to the chambers of commerce, save the " Manchester Guardian," the virtual completion of the scheme of underground telegraph wires which Lord Londonderry in the early part of the year premised should be carried out in all the principal storm centres between London and Scotland. The mains are now laid along three now sections on the west coast route. The three are the most exposed sections en the route between London and Elinburgls and Glasgow. The first is from Stafford to Warringtos, the seamad from Preston to Preston Richard, which is about ten miles north of Lancaster, and the third is along the steep incline on the London and North-Western Railway Trim Kendal Is Slap. Underground wires already ealsted from London to Stafford and from Liverpool to Mau:heater, so that the completion of the line from Stafford to Warringtoa places underground wires at the disposal et the Post-offieo from London to both Man- chester and Liverpool. The mains on all three sections are now laid, though the cables have net yet been taken thrones the whole of them,and indeed it is net intended to plies the cable in the, Kendal-Skap section this year. A great deal ef the cable teas, however, bean laid in the Stafford-Warrington section, and tie work of laying the cable is being proceeded with, as rapidly as possible in that from ?rest in to Preston Richard. The completion of these seetioos, the \ Post Office oflioials hope' will make the complete severance of Glasgow and 'Edinburgh, and indeed the whole of Scotland, a practical impossibility, for should the lines from Kendal to Shop be broken a coople of days work would be all that was necessary to place four gutta- petcha covered lines in the mains already laid, while experience has shown that along the other 'motion the chances of breakage are very ramote. The newly con- structed unde-ground Lnes are not, however, in any way intended to supersede the preseot overhead wires, ard in ordinary times they will be completely idle. Uoderground wires have been found to be much less efferitive and much more expensive to maintaia than overhead wires. The induction on them is a very serious matter, even en the best paper-covered lines, and con- sequently the uoderground wires are only to be used when there is great pressure of business or when the overhead wires are broken down.

As to further extensiens,they are intended te be Made next year on an oven larger scale than this year, but all in tile way of reserve wires, for use only on special occasions. The Post-effice preposes,7,if it can obtain the money from the Rouse of Commons, to make complete the underground °sensation between London and Paisley by connecting Warrington and Preston Richard and Keadal and Shap with Paisley. Two lines win braneh off at Paislr y. see to Edinburgh and the other to Glasgow. It may be that later on some extensions may made from Paisley to other points in tile South of Scotland, but that will not be just yet, and it is much or likely that the Post•offics will lay overhead wires to these place from Pal3loy, Glaggew and Edinburgh,se as to duplicate reutes in such a manner that in case ttierr.is a brealt4own oao way It is more than likely to be possible by another route to reach the required destination.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The Enteric Fever Outbreak at Winwick Asylum.

--- The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Be wsev Chanel:ors on Wednes- day afternoon. There were present :—Mr Joshua Ball (Presiding), Dr Murray, Mesers Halton, Houghton, Smoke, Mather, and Forshaw, with Dr Sephten (medi- cal officer), Messrs J C Sutton (clerk), S Sutton (assist- ant clerk), F Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B S Ne weotnbe (surveyor), and HM Burnage (assistant surveyor). GRANT FROM THE LICAL GOVERNMENT BOARD. The CLERK reported the receipt from the Local Government Beard of £239 7s 101 being the half-yearly grant under the Agricultural Rates Alt. TEE LIGHTING OF PADGATE. The CLERK informed the Couucil that there had been looms dispute about a claim sent by the Corporation for £4O 153 7d in respect of the laying of new gas mains in Green-larte,Palgate,eccasioned by the diversion of the road by that Couneil. He interviewed the Town:Clerk and the'GarEngineer with a viewfto coming to an arrange anent. There was no doubt that something was due from the Council because/it was at their instance that the road was altered and the mains had to be laid along it. He maintained that the Council were not liable to the cost of the mains, but inasmuch as owing to the alteration of the road there had been the labour of laying the mains, he made an offer for the Council to pay the cost of the labour. The Town Clerk and Water Esteineer accepted that arraneernent,and the effect would be that instead of having to pay over £4O the Council would have to pay only about £lO.

At the request of the Ginned he inspected the brook at Burtonwood from Mr Forshaw's to below the sewage works, and found the water quits clear and clean except near the brewery. On the day of his visit the tank at the brewery was being emptied and some of the sewage passed without being precipitated.
