The CLERK reported that the promoters of the ne electric express intended to make a start in the con- struction of the line, by laying six miles of rails in the Council's distriat. This section would be completed before any other part was proceeded with. He supposed the surveyor would have to watch the conruction of the line in the district on behalf of the Conn I.

THE TELEGRAPH POLES AT WINWICK. It will be remembered that at the last mewing of the Council a resolution was passer] requesting ths Surveyor Co communicate with the anthorities to ascertain if the I telegraph poles alongside the Winwick Asylum wall I could he removed. The Surveyor said it appeared that when the poles were erected the Council agreed to them being placed in their present position. The County Surveyor was of the opinion that if they were now re- moved the Council would be charged with the cost, as the autheritiea would have power to charge them with it. He thought, however, that if the authorities were properly approashed they might be induced to put the wires underground. The Council decided to take no action in the matter for the present.

A letter just to hand from Bermuda says that the writer is a torpedo man, and his duties were taken up with guarding the B3er prisoners, of which there were several thousands there. Every night lae kept a watch, burning a searchlight all round the islands. For the first two or three months he used to reei anyhow the next day, but one of his churns recommended Vi-Cocoa. For a time he used it, and after a week or so found that the fatigued feeling bad entirely disappeared, and he new says that it is Vi—Cocoa that sustained him and his mates through tha cold nights of last winter. _ Mr T J Brown, H.M.S. •Medina," Bermuda, West Indies, who writes this letter rightly adds "This is not a light task for ten months at a atretch..'
At Solihul on Tuesday Mr Harvey Du Cris was fined £2 and costs for drivinx a motor car at 35 miles an hour. The car was said to be the fastest in the world.

Few people realise the magnitude of the work under taken by the late Dr Drouet in the intereets of those who suffei from defective hearing and diseases of the ear. Besides creating large establishments in London, Paris, and 8rU11140,9, where aural ailments are treated by the Drouet method, he also founded a medical magazine, " The Journal for the Deaf," intended solely for the benefit of those who suffer from these sfffictions. This publication contains in each iesui valuable information on the care of the ears, and expressions of opinion by • various authorities on the curability of deafness. In- teresting instances of the cure cf deafness in al: its fornas are also given each month in the form of a Siplment " which contains the monthly records of the Drosset Institute. A free copy of Vie " Journal " and " Suppleme.nt " can be olo'•innd by addressing, the Secretary. Drou6t Institute. 72, Re•sen.'s Park-road, London, NW. With the " Journal "he always enclosed a Report 1,-,rm which enable anyone to reseive, free advice by corresnondesee as to the treatment of the ear, nose and throat.

div.head: Clericalism and Education.
div.p: Clericalism and Education.

Sir,—Romanisto are clamouring for help trona the public purse for their sehools. There is a suspicion in some' quarters that the Bill, before the country, will further endow sectarianism. The following quotation from the " Catholic Review" of April, 1871, supports Protestants in their view : "We do not indeed prize as highly as some of our countrymen appear to do, the ability to read, write, or cipher. Some men are born to be leaders, and the rest to be led." Precisely ! Father T J Ring, chairman of the West Hare School Board, has admitted that, in the matter of secular instruction, Catholic schools are "at the fag end." Yours &c. A. LE LIEVRE, Protestant Press Agency. 132 Wanstead Park-road, Ilford. 30th Ootober, 1902.
Education. The Rector and Mr. Henry Broadhurst.

Sir,—At the opening sf a sale of work in connection with the Pariah Church Restoration Fund, the Rector Canon Willis, referred to the Education Demonstration recently held in the Parr Hall. He spoke, we believe, in no unkind spirir,of "bearing an uneducated man—he called him an uneducated man, because the speaker said he was uneducated—who sooke with great eloquence and could move the masses." What Mr Broadhurst said was, that one of the chief reasons why be as a working man took such a deer; interest in the education question was due to the fact that having been born in a rural village sixty years agotwhen there was no School Boards, education was difficult for poor children to obtain. And than he spoke of the handicap this had been to him in life, and of his desire that the children of the workers of this day should not be burdened with this disadvantage. But at whose door lies the blame that such powerful natural intellects have during the last century been neglected, and handicapped by want of elementary education ? Doubtless there was not that general appreciation of knowledge that there is to-day, still as far back as 1807 the House of Commons paseeda Bill introduced by Mr Whitebread which pro- posed to provide a school for every parish, the cost te be defrayed out of the rates, and the management to be under the control of the ratepayers. This Bill passed the Commons, but met with bitter opposition in the Lords. The Archbishop of Cairerbury of that day said of it " This Bill left little or no control to the minister in his parish. This would go to subvert the first principles of education in this country which had hitherto, and h 3 trusted would continue to be, under the control and auspices of the Establishment." And on his advice and that of his colleagues the Bill was thrown out. The attitude of the Clerical party ef the Church of England has been to thwart every attempt of the State to promoteelernentary admiration through the medium of local administration and public control. Provided it was " under the con- trol and auspices of, the Establishment " they would accept it, but any control apart from their own they have resisted to the utmost of their flower. A Church writer in " Blackwoods Magazine " 1839 opposed the '• Education of the peeple on the grounds that it would make them uneasy and restless ; that ignorance was the parent of contentment ; and that the only education that could be fully given was a religions education , which renders them patient, humble and moral, and relieves the hardships of their present lot by a prospect of a bright eternity." So thought and so acted the Church at the time when young Broadhurst canoe into the world, arid if it be that he now suffers from any lank of education, the blame 'a with the Church oi who during the greater part of last ceatury opposed every effort made by the State to found a national system of education, unless that system was managed entirely by themselves. And for the credit of the Church She less the elergy call attention to the educational deficiencies of those who had bumble beginning during the earlier pert of last century, the better. One is elad to remember that there are times in the history of the Church when she has stood for the people's rights and liberties, and has held the lamp of learning high. But in regard to popular education, the Church of England's attitude during the last two centuries has bee; one of determined and sustained hostility. Sydney "Smith says :—" There is no protest- ant country in the world where the education of the poor has been so grossly and infamously neglected as in England."_ _ . _ - -

_ Frederick Denieon Maurice,himself a clergyman of the Establishment, and one who stood in the front rank of the thinkers o f last century says in his f.,,etures on El- ucation :—" There has been a heavy debt simewhere— granted : Ist us not attempt to hide it. The clergy have had the heaviest share in the evil. Let this be confessed both secretly and publicly." lam stating what every student of the social history of the English people during the last two centuries can test and prove for himself. We doubt not that it was the honest opinion 9f the leaders of the Church that to allow anyone to educate the poor in anything but the principles of the Establish- ed Church would be a danger to religion and to the State. But because their opinion was honestly held does not alter or excuse the fact that they have been the chief obstacle to the :educational advance during modern times'' _

_ Tho Rector went on to say in reference to the Parr Hall meeting " That the speakers also said that in many schools the managers wore only anxious to get • Churchman, a Catholic as they called him, to teach the doctrines, and that the managers did not care in the least about secular education, Re, the Rector, said that was utterly false." And se say I, but I also say it is utterly false " for the Renter to say that such a state- ment was made by any speaker in the Parr 11%11. Probably what the Rector refers to is what I myself sopremsod in the following words when speak- ing of the denominational sYstem. "Its main weakness ariees from the fact that it is controlled by those whose chief interest is not education, but religion, who in a great many cages and in a great many ways sacrifice educational interests for ecclesiastical ends, who work the schools in the interests of their denominational eye- term" This is a very different thing to saying that the church manners do not care in the least about secu- lar education. They may or may not be good educa- tionists, but they are, from the very conditions of their appointment first Churchmen or Wesloyans, as the case may be, and secend educationists. No reference was made by me to churchmen, it was the system I Condemned and not any particular church. The word catholic to which the Rector appears to object,oecurs jn a reference to a letter of a church visar to an applicalet for the position of teacher, which asked amonest other things whether the applicant was an early and frequent communicant ? Whether he played the organ ? What voice he sang in ? And stated that he must be a good Catholic ! This letter confirms what I said in regard to the denominational system and I could fiil your paper were it neoessary with other illustrations in connection with both fllaurcla and Nonconformist sehoole. rho R otor goes on to say " Of course they wanted thorough churehmen (as teachers) because they knew the teach- ing of the church was simply the teaching of the Bible— they knew that for a fact." I was in the company of a Plymouth brother the other day, and we had a Baptist with us. The first named with New Testament in band, with deep oarnest- neS9 of manner, sought to prove to us that the teachings of the Plymouth brethren were simply the teachings of the Bible, he knew that for a fact, and confirmed it ty a very powerful array of scripture texts, interpreted to , his own satisfaction. My Baptist friend and I listened at first with polite attention, but we soon grew weary because we etch knew that our special church teachings were the teachings of the Bible, we knew that for a fact, and could prove it each to his awn satisfaction. We parted good friends each respecting the conviction of the other. If the Rector of Warrington had joined our party and stated that he knew for a fact, that the teaehing of his Church was the teaching of the Bible,we
"I think FORCE ' is the best breakfast food I ever used. I would not go without it for anything."
(Name furnished on application.)

should have respected his convictions. But if he had I On the strength of those convictions and with the associa- tion and sanction of the State attempted to press those teachings upon our little ones, either personally or by deputy, we should have said hands off." And this we say in respcct to the Bill which the 11,ctor desires to be passed " not because they thought it would give them anything like that which they ought to have, but they thought it was the best Bill they could get." The Bill is uniest at its very foundation, and men like Henry Broadhurst, the stonemason's son, although not educated snd cul- tured in the sense that the Rector of Warrington under- stands education and culture, yet has a powerful grasp of those things which are et.ruilly right, or eternally wrong, and knows well that no law based upon injustice oan endure in a freedom-loving country. I have no desire to speak other than with respect of the Rector Personally, or of his honest and arduous work in connec- tion with the Warrington Day Schools. But belisving as we do that be, and every other denominational manager, is in a false and illogical position in forming part of a national, compulsory, and State-pail system of education, we will not shrink from shewing wherein this dual control of the State and the Churches works to ths detriment of the commonwealth, and the coatmon weal.
PPnketb, Novembr 4th, 1902.
CHARLES E. PARKER.

div.head: TRAMWAYS.
div.p: THE TRAMWAYS.
The Danger of Tower Waggons.
Warrington Man Killed. Fatal Fall in Scotland road.

George Merited& 35,Mersey•street. stated that be was employed by Messrs Blackwell and Co., as foreman linesman. On Friday afternoon Jones, himself, and an- other man were erecting guard wires over the electric tram trolley wires in Scotland-road, and they were us- ing a tewer waggon which was about 18ft high. The standing area at the top was sft. wide, lift. long, and there were 18 inches as a prstection. During the opera- tions the" pull-ovor," which was made et gun metal broke, and Jones was struck in the stomach and knocked off the_waggon. The Coroner, after inspecting the broken "pull-over expressed the opinion that it was a very bad casting. Be would like to knew how the moo were protected from falling off the waggon ? Mr Browne By being in their propet places. We shall prove that the deceased was in his wrong place. The Coroner (to witness) : What is there on this nlat- form to protect anybody if anything unforseen happens? —Witness: There is nothing. Mr Sisal: lbw long have you been working for Messrs Blackwell and Company 2—Witness : Five years- Mr Steel: When you are working on the tower waggon the work is all overhead, and to have a protec- tion around the platform would not hinder you from dolled your work 2—Witness : No. Da you suggest Jones was in his wrong place ?—h: don't know whether he was or not. He was all °"r t waggon. Was he in his right place or was he in his wrong. , place ?—lite was on the wrong side of the waggon. Where should he have been P—On the right side of the wire. Did you tell him he was in his wrong place 2—No. The Coroner: Do you think this man was doing 5115'" 1 thing wrong when he came ty the accident 2—Witness : No. Mr Steel : Do You think the waggon is safe without rails round the top as protectors P—There are other waggons that have rails on. Mr Barlow (coroner's officer) remarked that the Warrington Corporation waggon had protestors all round. Mr Steel : The men themselves have made a tempo- rary rail to go round P—Witness : Yes,lB iLches high. Mr Browne : Is there not a permanent rail around the top of this waggon, 18 inches high 2—Witness : Not right round, but on three sides. Mr Browne : You could not work on the fourth side if there was any protection, could you ?—No. Mr Browne : Did you ever see one with protection on the fourth side 2—Yes, at Leeds. Mr Browne : The only one 2—Yee. By the Coroner : Was there any protection on the side the deceased tumbled over 2—Witness : No.
Mr Browne : Didn't you hear the asaistant engineer warn the deceased two days before the accident about being on the wrong aide of tae wire ?--Witneso : Yee I did.
Mr Browne : The deceased bad no right to be on the near side of the wire where then was a strain P—That is so.

_ Par Browne : Had be any right to be where he was whelk he was kdleal ?-110 was in his wreng place. The Coroner remarked that it was clear there was nothing to incriminate anybody, but if the mater waS taken to a civil court there wbeid be a ro of conten- tion. Mr Steel would coutend that his client was the most innocent person in the world, and Mr Browno would contend that he was the most negligent of per- sons. If the jury were satisfied that no person was criminally to blame they were entitled to stop and say that it was an accident. His opinion was thst the jury were entitlel to find their verdict then, and if they took his advice they would not have any comment on it at all. Let the parties fight it out in the civil court if they wished. _ _ _

Mr Browne: The Workmen's Compensation Act does not apply, The Coroaer : Oh ! doesa't it: Mr Steel : Something else may apply though. The Coroner : I think you will both agree that what I ha ye said to the jury is right.. . _

T he jury havini co-nsidered the case,the Foreman re- marked that the jury were of opinion that the comparlY should provide a little better protection for the men working on this tower. Mr Browne : I don't to int;erfere but I have got , ample evidence here to prove that it is not necessary. I The Coroner : Put them into the box then. Mr F Higginson, chief engineer for Messrs Blackwell and Company, was then called. He stated that it was ' the general rule that no one must work inside" che curve," and there was a curve at the point where the deceased met with the aecident. If Jones had been on the outside of the curve he would not have been caught and thrown off the waggon* fie (witdes.9 preferred to werk on a waggon that had no protection. The only protection they could got was about 18 inches high. In answer to Mr Steel, witness said the Warrington Corporation waggon, which had protection, was used chitTly •r 1 I 9 ',l'll JI Ill.: The Coroner said the witness Edwirds had not crated a good impresaion on his mind. Edwards was the fore- man and knew whether Jones was doing right or wrong, and why did he not say so in the box ? 12 he was afraid of his employers, he ought not to be. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental Death and made a recommendation that they thought better p retection should be provided on the tower waggons b y the employers.

Another Asylum to be Built. div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL.

At the fortnightly meeting,beld on Tivsdav at Dutton Workhouse, there were present Messrs W Knowls (chairman), 9 Woodward (vice-chairman), Admiral Parry, H Talbot, J.P., T Baxter, C.C., J M A G Guest. r Lewis, J T Collier, T Darlington, J ' Mclntyre, J Spruce, G Pilling, C E Limaker, T Wright,J Balshaw, E Clarke, H Mandsley, P Gieave, J Nickson, R Billintnn, J Mounfield,T Antwiss,G F Ashton (clerk), W E Hough ((eputv clerk), W Adams (medical officer), J Farrington (inspector) and W Diggle and J Swinton (surveyor). THE THELW ALL NUISANCE.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL IN ACTION.-A VOLUME FROM MR. NAYLOR.
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL IN ACTION.-A VOLUME FROM MR. NAYLOR.

Referring to the alleged nuisance frona the tanneries, Mr Potts, clerk to the County Council, intimated that the County Medical Officer had been instructed to con- fer with the Medical Officer of the Rural Council with a view to a further investigation of the cause of the nuisance.

In a further communication Mr Potts irquired whether the Rural Council. under Section 25 t 5) of the Local Government Act, 1894 obtained any of the powers and duties of Urban authorities with respect to Grappenball and Thelwall and whether those Powers included dealing with nuisances arising from offensive trades. _ _

Mr Potts also forwarded letters respecting the nuis- ance from Mr H G Roberts of the LAcester Wesleyan Mission,who said the smEll made him sick during a visit last year ; and from Mr E Tinbull, Ashby Villa. Grappenhall who wrote corroborating the statement of Mr Leach the coachman, as to the abominable smell and the sickness from which the children suffered.

A report by Dr Vacher, County Medical Officer on the subject, submitted that neither on September 6th nor on any previous occasion when he visited Messrs. Long's tannery was he able to detecil apy effluvium other 1 than which would be produced at a tannery conducted in a proper and cleanly manner. That from the evid- ence of Mr Naylor`and members of his household and others,very bad effluvium nuisances have been caued from time ito time. That such ffluvium nuisances, it proved to have arisen from Messrs. Long's tannery must have been due to animal matter being exposed and allowed to decompose &T., or to the ffluent being in- sufficiently treated. That such effluvium nuisance, if due to an insufficiently treated Effluent is now being abated by the action of the officers of the Mersey and Irwell Watershed Committee. That such effluviuna nuisance if due to some other cause, than the effluvium from a bad effluent should be dealt with by the Runcorn Rural District Council.

Mr Leah wrote,giving a long history of his connection with Tbelwall, in the course of which be referred to the deaths of his three children from diphtheria. He said that since that cruel time he and his wife had been ' made ill many a time by the vile stench from the tannery, and it had been no uncommon thing for them to get up in the night for fear of sufhcation. They felt in the end that flight was their only safety, as they were agreed not to sleep any more in the vile smells. Mr Lrah wrote on a later date, stating in reply to Mr Linaker, that the stench still came on the Cuerden Hall premises as vile as ever. Mr Naylor had forwarded to the Council and to each member of the Council, a bulky.quarto volume of 45 pages, entitled " A summary of the complaint re The!- wall Nuisance." When the Clerk asked if he should read the book, there WRS a smiling response of" no." On the proposition of Mr Woodward, seconded by Mr Pilling, 'the Medics' Officer was instructed to meet Dr Vacher, and that the various officers affordevery facility to the inquiry. Mr T Baxter said it had been suggested that a watch should be set at night, as it was alleged that the objec- tionable discharge took place principafly during the night time. The County Council Health Committee had given Dr Vacher a free hand to try and unravel the mystery._ . .

_ Mr Mclntyre said in Mr Naylor' s publication it was stated that he (Mr Mchtyre) bad said that if Dr Penny's report condemned the tannery the C)uncil would call in another expert. This was an unmitigated—he would not say a lie, but it was far from the truth.'He would as soon pledge the wind as pledge a Council of over 40 bigb spirited gentlemen. (Hear, hear.) At the instigation of Mr Woodward the Council testi- fied their confidence in Mr Mclntyre. The discussion there ceased the Chairman remarking that they seemed te have got into form now that the Councils Medical Officer and the County Medical Officer were meeting on the subject.
ADMIRAL PARRi'S INTERROGATORIES.
Admiral Parry asked the following questions :- 1 Is carchpit behind Bark Shed finished to satisfac- tion of Medical Officer of Health ? 2 How much of Waste-lane drain has been relaid ?

3 Has 27pb0n or Flap Valve been placed at terminus of one fcot and two ft. pipes? 4 Has any authority been given to Road Surveyor to employ men inside tanyard property, or in taking in a portion of Mr Naylor's ground, and is there any plan of such work?
5 How much has been paid this financial year for macadam or chippings outside the contracts laid before the Council?

The rephee were (1) no; (2) none at present; (3) no (4) Medical Officer's instructions ; (5) nothing but what has been in the Surveyor's requisitions. In regard to the first question Mr Mclntyre told the Council to put the cost down to Belmont estate. It was decided that no work should be stopped by any official without notice being given to the Councillor of the district.
THE PROPOSED ISOLATION HOSPITAL.

The Hospital Committee recommended that two archi- tects prepare preliminary plans, and that the architects meet the committee on the site for the purpose of hearing their views as to the style of building. The Clerk, in answer to Mr Baxter, said there was provision for 24 beds in the administrative block and 12 in the Isolation Hospital proper. This was in accord- ance with the suggestion of the County Medical Officer. 1 Mr Woodward moved the adoption of the report and said the hospital could be extended as required. Mr Wright seconded. A propessl by Mr Talbot to engage one architect only Was not seconded. Mr Woodward said they would probably save more than the cost of the plans by being able to compare two sets of pane. The committee's report was approved. LAPWING LANE.

Mr T B Greenwood, engineer of the Runcorn division of the Ship Canal, wrote informing the Council he could hot undertake to fence a portion of Lapwing-lane as desired.. There was no obligation on the Company to do this. If the Council desired to extend their new fence up to the bridge no objPction would be made. Mr Swinton said to fence the portion of the road belonging to the Ship Canal Company would cost £22, and the who's, of the work £56.
Several members considered the road in its present state to be dangerous
It was ultimately decided tc again approach the Ship Canal Company and inform them that the Old Quay Company kept the fence in repair.

div.head: GOLDEN WEDDING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: GOLDEN WEDDING AT RUNCORN.

Last Friday Mr and Mrs Joseph Littler, of Water- loo-road, celebrated their golden wedding, having been married on October 3lat, 1852, in the Parish Church of Great Iludwortb. Mr and Mrs Littler ' have lived for the greater part of their married life in Runcorn, and are widely known and highly respected. The members of the family assembled at their home on Friday to commemorate the intereatiog occasion, and, with the exception of the only son, Mr Wilson W Littler, who for many years past hae resided in Rockhampton, Queensland, all the children and a number of the grand-children of the esteemed couple were present.

div.head: CAUEIi FOR OBEiCENITY,
div.p: A CAUEIi FOR OBEiCENITY,

On Monday, John Owen, of Runcorn, appeared before the magistrates for using obscene language on October 27tb. In defence be said be bad been asleep on the sofa and was awakened b 3 two men coming in the house. They told him they had orders to remove everything that belonged to his wife, and were proceeding to do so when he pro- tested. They therefore put him on the floor and one of them sat on his sornach for quite two hours while the other, assisted by his wife's daughters and sons, removed the furniture and other articles. They took some of his belongings and left some of his wife'a. His wife afterwards demanded all that belonged to her, and on her returning what be owned he gave her what had been left. She had not been in the house since. He admitted using obscene language, but said he was provoked to do so.—The magistrates advised him to consult a solicitor about the conduct of the men, and fined bim 10a for using obscene language.

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By 00valisi]

Warrington lost at Hull on Saturday by one goal, two tries to one goa', one try, the winning point being gained very unexpectedly by the home team in the last five minutes. There is no gainsaying the fact that the result is very disappointing, even though the defeat is not at all a severe one, because nearly everybody here , expected the locals to assert their superiority over the Hull men. That they possess that superiority there is , no question even now, but as it all lies in the backs ' and the forwards had the worst of the argument it was not much use on Saturday. Warrington played a really good game and deserved to halve the points at least. Hull were very keen on winning, however, and it was just an extra unlooked-for effort that pulled them through. We must admit that the " Third Porters " accomplished a good performance seeing that they were without Taylor, the county full back.

Would Warrington have won had they made the journey on Friday? is a question which a number of people are asking. Personally, lam unable to say, but the probabilities are that the men would have been fresher and more inclined for the severe struggle which awaited them The Hull people themselves consider that the long journey which most of the visiting teams have to make is a very strong point in favour of the homesters. If Warrington could have ensured two points by going on Friday then they ought to have gone, but the question is one which the committee alone have to decide, and I presume they acted for what was the best in their view.

The cheap fare on Saturday encouraged a good number of Warringtonians to accompany the team on their long journey,but they cannot have obtained much gratification from their visit, because following a losing team is not the most cheerful of pleasures. However, Warrington have not started the season at all badly, and there is good reason to expect that they will show an improvement on previous records when once the curtain has dropped.

Hull tried a new man on Saturday in R W Jackson, a sprinter, and a player of many clubs, and like new men often do, he won the match. A.draw seemed inevitable until Jackson was left uncovered, and getting a timely pass he raced in with nothing to spare. Previously the scoring had been level. Hull started with a penalty goal, and then W.rrington replied with some beautiful combined work, which resulted in Isherwood scoring in good position and Fish placing a goal. Morgan got in for Hull with an unimproved try ere the interval arrived, and it was "five all "until Jackson did the trick at the end of the game. Hull were certainly going strongly at this stage, their forwards lasting better and overplaying Warrington in the scrummages. Otherwise the boot would probably have been on the other leg, for the Warrington backs were always the more dangerous set when the ball came their way.

It is a great pity, I think, that the fine back division Warrington now possesses should be handicapped by want of strength among the forwards. I would not for a moment blame the latter, they have played magnifi- cently this season, but they lack weight and it is quite evident that their exertions are beginning to tell. The majority of teams Warrington meet are considerably heavier and more powerful in the forwards, so that the strain of holding their own must be a most severe and unequal one for the Warrington pack to withstand. I am confident that with two or three men of Boardman's stamp in the front rank Warrington would be a most formidable team, with att ;eking powers largely en- hanced through increased opportunity. Look at the position of Salford, for instance. They have won more matches than we have with a back division not to be mentioned in the same breath with our own. Their success is entirely due to super-abundant forward strength without which they would have little chance to score. It was only their controlling power here that enabled them to beat Runcorn on Saturday, and they beat Warrington for the same reason. One does not like to grumble, especially after a defeat, but I watched the "A "team on Saturday and was only too well and sadly convinced of Warrington's weakness forward. The "A" teamers made a ho-rible show in the packs against such a junior organization even as Leigh St. Joseph's, arid there was not one of them fit for a reserve in first-class football. The backs, with the ex- ception of Edmunds, are little better,but that is not the point at issue. We want forwards first ! I see Swinton got a good scrummager last week in R. Yates of Wigan, by the simple process of swapping a spare half back for him. This shows that the men can be got ! Forwards are not quite as scarce as backs, and I should imagine some of the down-on•their-luck second-league teams would be glad to do a deal in money or kind. The Rangers purchased Oram and Trotter from Stock- , I port. Cannot we buy in the same or some adjoining I market?

Isherwood was the best man on the Warrington side, his play being characterised by that reliability which is his strong forte Fish was quite off colour and was nothing like so resourceful and speedy as of yore. So far, this season, Fish does not seem to have shakdn down into his best form and he has done very little scoring. Harris might also have been better and it was through him, I understand, that Jackson was allowed to score the winning try, while his failure to stop Hodgson in the Cheshire match is alleged to have spoiled his chance of being preferred to Hogg against Yorkshire. Knight had little to do at Hull, but he played a fair game.

There is now only one undefeated team in the League —Halifax, who possess a clear lead of three points over any rival. They have hal some very easy matches so far, and I await with interest their entry into Lanca- shire. Runcorn went down on Saturday before Salford, who only obtained the majority of points by success- ful goal kicking. Swinton and the Rangers both won, Batley and Bradford being the victims, and both had good men assisting Yorkshire County.

The Northern League table up-to date is as follows: For. Agst. P. W. L. 11. G. T. P. G. T. P,Pra• Halifax 9 8 0 1 914 60 6 0 10 17 Swinton Broughton It Leigh 9 6 2 113 12 62 512 46 13 Salford Runcorn Warrington 9 4 3 2 810 46 9 9 45 10 Oldham Bradford Hull Wigan Batley Huddersfield St Helens Widnes .19 14 62 4
Hull K Rovers 9 2 7 0 2 6 22 12 17 'A a Hunslet Brighouse Rgs

Yorkshire easily defeated the Cumbrians, who were handicapped by accidents uring the play, one of which, lam very sorry to say, has terminated fatally. One rarely hears of anything so serious in Northern Union football, but accidents will happen anywhere. The unfortunate player was J. 11 Richardson, the smart Whitehaven half back, who hurt his groin by a collision with one of his fellow players in the Cumberland team. Though he resumed he had to be taken to the Leeds Infirmary at the end of the game. Here it was dis- covered that a dangerous operation would be necessary, and on Monday he succumbed. Footballers and sports- men generally all over the country will be saddened by so unhappy an event.

I There has been a lot of fuss about Warrington's match with Broughton Rangers on the 15th when the Rangers will have to find five men for the County team. Doubtless it is hard on the Rangers, but on Saturday they got an easy two points out of Bradford, whose best Imen were representing Yorkshire, so that the matter cuts both ways. The League Committee have done quite right in refusing the application of the Rangers for a postponement of the Warrington fixture. It is not Warrington's fault, but the fault of the system which compels League clubs to furnish their best men for the County when they are wanted in competition football. Warrington will, of course, be without Fish and possibly Boardman, but the Rangers are un- doubtedly afraid of the remainder. What I fear is that we shall hear at the last minute that Wilson or Hogg has missed another quarter, and Harris or Dickenson will be called upon. This would tend to equalise matters Broughton way, and they know a thing or two at Wbeater's Field. However we shell see what we shall see on the the 15th.

To-day the ever-popular encounter with Oldham comes off at Wilderspool, and, of course the locals are expected to win. Oldham hare had the worst of their en- gagements with the wire-pullers in recent years,and last season lost four points to Warrington, but they always provide a good game. Formerly they used to outclass all opponents in the back division, bu times have changed and warrington can probably put a better rear division in the field than most clubs, Oldham in- cluded. Some of the men—the two centres for instance —are nem' to Warrington and their form will be watched with interest Oldham are said to be strong forward this 'rear and another big effort will be called for from the Warrington eight.

div.head: Letters to the Editor.
div.p: Letters to the Editor.

Sectarian Strife in Runcorn—who is responsible. Sir,—Me George Haziehunt saddled the wrong horse when at the church bazaar he referred to the unhappy sectarian strife. The difficulty is not that the Wesieyans refuse to follow Hugh Price Hughes, but that Canon Wood will not co-operate, in Christian work, even with this reverend gentleman. Having acted as local seer,- tary for the West London Mission during the visit of 1891, permit me to refresh the memory of your readers on toe subject. The mission was accorded the heartiest welcome by men of all creeds, and the clergy, including Dr Preston. late vicar of Holy frinity readily appeared oa the plat- form. Canon Wood, however, riot only refused to do so, but trorn the parish pulpit warned his peopi, against attending. His sermon published in his magazioe at the time,reads as follows : " And this leads ins after much careful consideration to venture to sug- gest t) you, as loyal churchpeople, that it will be wiser and better to avoid giving support to such religkus effoit outside your own church, as you are now invited to countenance and assist. If Igo and take my place upon a Wesleyan or any Nonconformist platform, I thereby recognise their organization as forming a legitimate part of the Cathelic Church in this land. Now an instructed churchman cannot do this. He knows that the Saviour founded one visible Church under the apostles. Re believes that the Body called usually " The Church of Eagland "is for this country the oaly true, legitimate and historic branch of that one church and he cannot, therefore, for popularity or peace put on one side his conviction and admit that there are many churches." The sermon then proceeded Co deny the validity of ministerial orders and the authority of sacrameats otner than those of the Canon's "One Church" and even to argue that although the Almighty Himself allows such organizations to do good,it does not folltrar that they ought to be recegoi led as true branc‘,.lei of the Church.

The vigorous religious boycott the Canon theo preached he has since persistently practised, with the result that what was before his advent a happy com- munity of broad-minded Christiana ready to suppnt any work that bore God's seal of usefulness, is tirned into a cockpit of sectarian disputants, with its painful record of proselytising curates, divided famillei, parted friend- ship, and a civic life distrimted between the claims of the " One Church" and broad-minded citizenship. It is only fair to rea9rd that the leading churchmen of that day strongly protested against the introduction of such extreme narrowness into the religioui life of the town, and despite the Canon's boycott subscribed hand- somely to the mission. It will be wise for the present generation to acquaint themselves with these historical facts which reveal the root cause of all our sectarian strife and throw a flood of light on its subse- quent painful development. They must realise that the Csnor.'s creed compasses the capture or conversion of Roman Catholicism and Nonconformity alike. They must then determine it such medievalism, however sincere, is practical in these days, and whether it is worthy of their allegiance or no. In any case they must acquit all Churches outside the Canon's " One Church ' of all responsibility for the disastrous conse- quences to the social, civil and religious life of the t which have followed its introduction. That responsi- bility rests solely with the " One Church,"—Yours faithfully, FREDERICK JOHN NORMAN. Lyndhurst, Runcorn, November sth.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS
Result of the Poll,
A Non-Trading Triumph.

Tee question before the burgesses at the eleeion on Saturday was undoubtedly that of" municipal trading" Few subjects have been so fiercely debated in Warring- too is this one, and the verdict of the elector-ate, judged by Saturday's results, is against trading by members of the Council with the Corporation through limited com- paniea in which they are interested, There were conte4ts in six of the nine wards, and in each ward the Munici- pal Non-Trading Committee hi a candidate. The President of the Committee(Mr James Dodds)opposedthe return of Councillor Shilleock, who has represented the Town Hall Ward for the past nine years.At the outset,Mr Dodds announced his intention not to personally canvass a single burgess or ask for a single vote, but he had many friends who worked energetically on his behalf. Mr Shilleock canvassed personally and worked hard, but he had not as many workers as on former occasions. Votes were asked for him in a circular signed by 0 un- cillor Smethurst, chairman of the Conservative Ward C ommittee, and Mr James Strettle (hon secretary), and the following reasons were given why the electors should vote for the Conservative candidate, narnelyr—b ettli9 by voting for him "you vote for one of yourselvel ; for a man who resides in th 3 ward, and not three mil' s out of it; for a fair minded man who does not went to form his fads down everyone's throat ; for a man who has had nine years' experisn ; for a man who has nothing to sell to the Corporaticn, and svA has therefore no personal interest to serve, and for a man who upholds the honesty of the Town Council." In a " la3t word to the electors," the friends of Mr Dodds asked the electors to support him at the poll on the following •grounds :—" He represents large rate- payers and so would carefully watch expenditure. Ho has no axe to grind, and w ould oppose all improper and illegal trading by any member or members of the Council with the Corporation. He has shown his respect for you by abitaining from using any personal infl 1- eoce upon you ; that is, he has n c til ',ragged one or you him4elf, his; has 1 ,ft it to your conseience an un- biassed judgment as to whether or not he is deserving of roar sympathy and support." Polling proceeded cpaie.ly during the dar. There was a steady stream of burgesses to the polling station at Kendrick-street schoolroom and a heavy poll was anticipated. This was verified when the papers were counted at the Town Hall. In two of the Wards there was a thres-cornered fight. Mr A J J Aleylwas the retiring councilor in Fairfield ward and his return was challenged by Mr Craik,who holds the position'of Rectos's warden at the Parish Church,and Mr R Bolton, who had the support of the Municipal Non- Trading Committee.

Toe following "two plain reasons" why the burgess should vote for Mr Jolley were put forward :—(1) That he was a practical man who thoroughly understood mucicipal work, and (2) that be was a man who spoke plainly and meant what be said, who was an authority upon educational, poor low, and other important ques- tions which were beneficial to the working classes " Conservatives, who' make a change 2" was asked. all then the electors were entreated t "stink to the officio( candidate, who has honestly tried to do his bast to rep- resent you faithfully and well the last three years."—Mr Craik ainounced that he was independent of either political party, and was averse to members of the Coun- cil trading with the Corporation either directly or through limited corcapanies--An unfortunate accident occurred during the polling. Mr Philip Evans, of Manchester-road, WAR proceeding to the plling station at Fairfield schools, when a large board on which some placards were dis- played WAR blown down by the wind and in falling knocked Mr Evans down. It was found that Mr Evans had sustained an injury te his leg and Dr McCarthy was sent for by Mr Craik and attended to the injured limb. The popularity of Mr Craik in this ward was evidenced by the large number who recorded their votes on his behalf. Ile polled more than both his opponents Put together. The surprise of the contest was the small support accorded to Mr Jolley.

The triangular contest- in Hewsey Ward was hetween Mr Brophy (L),Mr S Gough(Non-Trader)and Mr Shawn Mr Brophy worked hard and was assisted by a number of staunch friends. Mr Gough and Mr Shaw had pre- viously contested the ward and there was some doubt as to the result. Mr Brophy's supporters, however' seemed confident of viotory, and as the result proved their confidence was not misplaced. Mr John Uoson,the Liberal candidate in 0 ford Ward had also the support of the Non-Trading Committee. As head-master of the Silver-street day schools he is well- known in the ward and his scholars showed their par- tiality for him by sporting his colours in their cave. It was difficult to forecast the result owing to the Catholic vote. The Rev Fathers Neville Wilson and John Baines, In asking for the support of Roman Catholics on behalf of Mr Robinson,the Conservative oandidate,sairl :—" We have had an interview with Mr James Robinson, and are pleased to say that he pledges himself, if roturned, to do his utmost to secure fair treatment from the educational authority, to be constituted under the Education Bill, for Catholic Sahools, and adeq late re- presentation of Catholics on the said authority." Mr Upson issued a rejoinder to the Roman Catholic electors by giving the following reasons for supporting him. (1) He has been a Voluntary School reacher for 20 year.. (2) He is in favour of the present Education Bill. (3) He refused to pledge himself to work for its withdrawal. (4) He was chairman of a large meeting of voluntary teachers in Manchester. who passed resolutions unanim- ously in favour of the Bill in June Isst. (5) He will endeavour to secure fair treatment to all Voluntary Schools, including, of course, Catholic schools. (6 Be is intimately acquainted with all the datails f the Bill (7) He has the ability to 'process his Views. (8) tin knows the needs of the Voluntary Schools thornughly,and will do his best to get justice for them, Mr Upson and his friends felt confident of success but few anticipated the triumph which was secured. The contest in St Austin's Ward was much keener than many anticipated. Mr Lord made a hold hid to wrest the seat from Councillor Tinnion, but he failed and was in a minority of 83. There was a lar7e nnmbar of absentee Liberal voters and no great orte we?, made to bring them to the poll. The figures show that over 300 burgesses did not record their votes. it 14 a striking commentary on the electien that Mr Tinnion is the only retiring Councillor who in the wards contetted on Saturday, was returned to the Council for another terns of office.

The contest in Latchford' Ward was one of the most' excitine which has ever been witnessed there. Mr John Pemberton, who was defeated last year by Coun- cillor Ellison, was successful in a remarkable degree, on this occasion. He was the official candidate of the Con- servative organisation and had also the support of the Non-Trading Committee, with which he has haen Prominently identified. His (moment was Mr W B Roberts. an independent Conservative and prominently connected with the brewery, of Meagre Gmtnsii. Whitler and Co. The Liberal Ward Committee gave their sup- port to Mr Roberts, but there seems to have been a great deal of crose voting on both sides. Mr Pemberton attitude on the coo-trading question made him popular with the electors, hot cow were prepared to hear of him being elected by 200 votes. THE COUNTING.

Immediately at the 0139/3 of the poll, the ballot boxes were sealed and conveyed to the Town Hall. The first box to arrive was from Cairo-strest echool- room,containing the votes of the eleeters in that portion of St Austin's Ward. Shortly afteirwar is the boxeS from the Town Hall Ward were received and counting was then proceeded with in the Town Hall in the Coml. cit Chamber. The proceedings were watched with intense interest by a large number of people. The rotes in St Austin's and Town Hall Ward were first counted. It was early seen that Mr Dodds had a suberactial majority in the Town Ball Ward arid when the votes bad been counted therm was general surprise at the largeness of his majority. 0911 hour and a half elapved before all the voting papers had been counted in the six wards. The results were announced in the room by the returning officers, and votes of thanks were then paesed. ecuneillor Tinnion thanked the Mayor, Town Clerk, and all the officials for the verr efficient arrangements which had been made for conducting the election in St Austin's ward, He remarked that the fight had been. hard one, but a fair one, and while he had the honour to represent the ward.and bad been selected by a major- ity of 83, be still thought his opponent had made a good fight. He concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to the Returning Officer (Alderman Shaw Green), Mr Lord seconded the vote of thanks which woe carried.

Alderman Shaw green in responding Raid ha hoped Olunci!tor Tinnion might long be spired to continue the very efficient services he had rendPred ro the bnrnugh. Councillor UPSON proposed a vote of thankq to Alder- man Hutchinson. the returning officer for the Orford Wsord. Hi 9 gond friend, Mr Robinson, and himself wore novicoe in the matter of a municipal fight, but he did not think they had committed any grave breachea of the proprieties Thor had been greatly aasisted by the presiding officer and the poll clerk Mr Roatnsox prannnd@ci, and the motion was carried.

Councillor UPSON, asked the comoany to spare him the anguish of making a speech hecauie,like Mr Brophy, he was physically overcome by the w rk he had done during the past week As tar as he remembered, his victory was the &nut that had ever been won in the ward. (Hear, hear.) He belleyed the majority of nearly two to one established a record. fle attributed that victory, not to himself, ha to the fact that be had the most splendid hand of workers that ever took the field in that ward. (Applause.) Be mast thank them in the heartiest manner for their assistance. For,as he put it to them the previous night, they we-e not voting for a person but a cause—(hear, hear)—and it was because they were voting for a cause, and that personality did not enter into the contest, that they had achieved their victory. He entered iato the contest with some reluct- ance, but having entered into it he had done his best to gain the day. (Applause.) HP had fought fairly and squarely, and he thought he would not have to be reproached for having hit below the belt. He bad been a member of that club ever since he came to Warring- ton, and he had worked for the Liberal cause for many years, both in Warrington and the county diylßims of Cheshire. He would not lack in his eff nts for the party which, he believe-1' to be the party of righteousness and purity. Re w..s determined to know no party in the Council, but he would work for the general good of the town and oppose everything that savoured of selfish- ness or of self-interest. (Applause ) He would try to seek the good of those people who had not sufficient representation in the Council—the p ,orest and the weakest. (Hear, hear.) He believed much might be done to better the lives of ordinary people in providing for their reasonable recreation. While they spent huge sums in various ways which, perhaps,they might object to, the expenditure of a few hundred pounds might bring happiness to thousands of little children who had nothing but the slums to play in. (Applause). Ho thanked all who had voted for him, and he was glad to sty he was not going to the Council for himself, but for them (Applause.) Councillor BROPHY returned thanks to his workers. A letter was received froaa—Rev Father Chambers, Runcorn, making the fcllowing request :—" Toat the burial of any Catlaolies who may in future die at the Workhouse. Mould take place in the Cstholic p )rtion of the Runcorn Cemetery instead of at Littla Leigh. His 84800 i for this were, that the latter place was so far from Rune srn rhs.t, though he was called upon to attend but few funerals it was a serious inconvenience, and sat:astir/les expense for nha to go [Me distance. Catholic people na- turally wished to be buried in a Catholic cemetery; when ever possible. The extra distance from Dutton to Run-. corn instead of Little Leigh was not considerable. When- ever those Cathone w: o died at Dutton had relations who were able to bear the expense of the funeral they were generally brought to Rincarn for burial. He miatit say he felt sot., that the B ,ard would not think this small favour t,o much to xpact for those who were not 'so fortunate. He felt sure the Board would see the reasonableneFs of this petition. The relations of dead. I Catholics bad frequently expressed their disappoint- ment a: n b -Mg able tobury their friends at the Catholic pO, too of Runcorn cemetery or elsewhere. In another letter the R-v tCer Caambers stated that the grave fees at R ,eaere Cemetery were 13s 6i for adults and 123 61 for tuf,‘ete Ind children under seven years of age. These oinoluded everything, but the fees were doubled in the Cats of peop:e outside Runcorn. He thoaght that special terms might possibly be arranged with the cemetery aut'mrities if the fees were higher than at Little Leigh.

Toe Clerk snid some carrespondence had passed between himself and Father Chambers who had sug- gested that special arrangements might be made with the Ruunorn Cemetery authorities. He (toe Clerk) therefore warted upon the clerk to the Urban Ciuncil, who said burials tram the Workhouse would be con- sidersd out-cases and double fees would be charged This would be 275. for adults. At Little Leigh the charge was 6a 2d. ("Oh.")
Baxtrer protested against special charges b.lng paid to convey bodies to Runcorn. • '
_ It was pointed out that these charges were outside the purchase of a grave and Douglas said a third class grave at Runcorra cost Z 153.

Mr -Woodward said he had received a letter from Dr Gil stabil asking him to SOP justice done in this matter. Be did not think this was a reflection on the Hoard. He did not think Mr Chambers proposal right. If relatives were desirous of a corpse being taken to Runcorn there was no objection,provided no greater coat fell upon the riu%rdians. At Runcorn the charge for a new grave and an interment was £2 12, and there would, in addi- tion, be an increased charge for c mveving the body to Runcorn. It was for the religious bodies to take the matter into considerati le and deal with it on equitable and fair lines and not ask the guardians to bear an extraordinary charge. Mr Williams moved that Father Chambers' request be not acceded to.

Mr Norman said pnrhaps Father Chambers did not expect the Guardians to pay more than they paid at Little Leigh. He moved that the Board were quite willing that the cases should be taken to Runcorn pro- vided that no more expense was incurred by the Guardians than an interment at Little Leigh would entail.

Mr Lea seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr Woodward said Dr Gastalii used to read the service in the mortuary and the funeral took its course afterwards. Perhaps Ur Chambers was mora enthusi- astic.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1902. TO THE BURGESSES OF BEWSEY LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I beg to tender my sincere thanks for the honour you have done me by placing me at the head of the Poll and also the band of Workers whose effarts contributed so largely in attaining that result. As your representative in the Town Council, 1 shall at all times do my utmost to further the best interests of all the Burgesses of the Ward—irrespestive of party—and to promote the welfare of tho]town generally. Again thanking you for the con- fidence reposed in me. I am yours faithfully, JOHN BROPHY. 2. Dallam-lane, Warrington. November 3rd, 1902.

AfUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, 1902. To THE Ail. BURGESSES OF THE HOWLEY WARD. LADIES AND OENTLEMEN,— For the second time you have been good enough to return me to the Council unopposed. I have for nine years striven honestly to further what appeared t, me to be the truest interests of the town,uninfluenced by party ties or thoughts of personal advantage. lam rewarded amp)y by this generous renewal of your confidence,which I shall labour with redoubled ardour to deserve. Faithfully yours, ARTHUR BENNETT. Warrington, 25th October, 1902.

Wigan-633, 8 15,9 26. 9 56, 10 0, 11 22, la 15, 1 25, 2 3 427, 25, 456, 5 20. 7 5, 9 0, 10 30. • STOCKTON HEATH. --- HILL CLIFFE AND STOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OF HOPE.-On Monday evening the second public meeting of the session in connection with the Band of Hope was held in the Providence Schoolroom. The chair was occupied by the President,the Rev J S Hughes,who was supported by the speaker of the evening, the Rev H Dunnico, who delivered an address on "The force of habit." A capital programme was given consisting of recitations by the Misses Edith Cole, Mary Earle, Lillian Hall, Maud Mortimer, Jessie Ellison, May Isher- wood, and Polly Brereton, and Masters G A Whitfield,H Nicholls, A Bailey, J Whitfield, and J J Worrell. Songs were well rendered by Miss Bell,Miss Winnie Jones,and Mister Stanley Jones. The Ebenezer Wesleyan Choir contributed two anthems which were much appreiiated. Mr A H Dunn was at the harmonium. A very appro- priate dialogue, " Guy Fawkes," was well given, whilst the humorous dialogue "The Irish schoolmaster " pro- voked roars of laughter. Warrington P.S.A. Society. Mr E Osborne presided at a meeting of this society in the Co-operative Mall, Sankey-street, on Sunday. Mr Oorrin sang "Look up, sad heart,' and "Eternal Rest " very effectively, being accom- panied by Mr Wadsworth. Mr W Light gave an address, for which he was warmly thanked. Buckley-street P.S.A. Society. On Sunday afternoon an open meeting of this society was held in the Alethodist Free Church, and was fairly attended. Mr Ellis occupied the chair, the speaker being Mr Cox (St Helens). Mr W Rich- ardson sang with good effect The Holy City," and Mr S Cook gave an excellent rendering of " Will you meet me at the fountain." Mr Albert E Trow was the accompanist. Death of Mr. Heber Taggart. The death occurred at Greyfriars. Chester, on Sunday morning of Mr Reginald Heber Taggart, assistant at Messrs Eustance and Co.'s jewellery establishment, Sankey-street, Warrington. Mr Taggart had been staying at Chester temporarily assisting Mr Butt his cousin, who is a jeweller, and on Tuesday week he was taken ill with pneumonia, from which he died, despite the attention of Dr Butt. Deceased who was 30 years of age, was the son of the Rev T A Taggart, vicar of St Matthew's Douglas. He gained many friends during his four or five years stay in Warrington, and was held in high esteem. He was secretary of the Nomad's Cycling Club and as highly respected by every member. The deceased's remains were conveyed to Douglas, his native place on Tuesday and interred at Onchan.
